title: Zero to RHCSA on RHEL 10
description: Begin with your first AlmaLinux login and build toward independent RHEL 10 administration. Practice in a live terminal beside each reading, solve shift assignments, and test your work on a two-machine RHCSA practice exam.

modules.title: Start here: meet your AlmaLinux machines
Learn how Bash reads commands and how to find help
Work with paths, text, links and backups
Manage identities, privileges and shared files
Connect the client and server by address and name
Manage signed RPM and Flatpak software
Observe running work, logs and performance
Turn repeatable work into Bash scripts
Provision disks, logical volumes and swap
Mount local storage and deliver remote files
Follow the boot chain and recover a practice guest
Rehearse, sit the practical and review the evidence
Optional extension after exam review: containers and image mode

lessons.title: Meet Linux and install your first practice machine
lessons.body:
A coworker tells you that the reports are missing from “the server.” Before changing anything, you need to know which computer holds the reports and how to ask it a question. In this course the **server** offers files and services. The **client** requests them. Both are computers running Linux. You will work on both sides of that conversation.

Linux is the **kernel**, the part of the operating system that manages devices, memory and running programs. A **distribution** packages the kernel with utilities, software and documentation. You will practice on AlmaLinux 10.3 and prepare for the RHCSA exam based on RHEL 10. A **virtual machine** (VM) is a whole guest computer with its own operating system and disk. The physical or virtual computer running Erudior is the host.

## Open your first guest

In Erudior Desktop 0.25.3 or later, select **Open practice terminal** above this reading. In **First-time setup**, follow the instructions for your host. The desktop can fetch the verified DVD and practice kit or accept both as local files. Select **Start lab**. The first build installs a base system and takes longer than later starts. Leave the app open until the machines are ready. The shared **Client console** opens when the client starts. Give it time to boot, then press Enter for the login prompt. Expand **Console login** for the username and the password for this attempt. At a Linux text login, typing the password displays no characters. Type it once and press Enter.

The reading and the terminal share the window. Click inside the terminal before typing. Press **F6** to switch focus back to the course or return to the terminal. The **Server console** button switches guests. The shared practice shell follows you to the next reading. Practical exam lessons supply separate machines for the assessment.

If you are reading in a browser, open your own AlmaLinux VM alongside it. The **Set up and reset the AlmaLinux 10.3 lab** reference walks through the two-machine kit. A browser-only reading session also lets you predict results and answer quizzes. Return to the terminal exercises when you have a guest.

[AlmaLinux 10.3 x86_64 DVD installer](https://repo.almalinux.org/almalinux/10.3/isos/x86_64/AlmaLinux-10.3-x86_64-dvd.iso) · [AlmaLinux practice kit](https://app.erudior.com/downloads/Erudior-AlmaLinux-10.3-Practice-Kit.zip)

## Ask three questions

In each transcript, a leading `>` marks text you type. Leave off the first `>` on each input line. A blank line means nothing was printed. Unmarked text shows sample terminal output. Longer listings may show selected rows. Names, addresses, dates, IDs and package versions reflect the example machine. For password prompts, type your own password when asked. Its characters stay hidden.

On the supplied client, sign in as `learner`. The first two commands print your login name and the guest’s network name. The last command prints the operating system release file. Its output below is an excerpt from AlmaLinux 10.3. A different account, guest or release will give different values.

Find `ID` and `VERSION_ID` in `/etc/os-release`. They identify the distribution and release. Switch to the server and predict which of these three answers will change. Check your prediction, then return to the client.

## Install a machine yourself

The managed desktop route has already built the machines. To learn installation hands-on, use a separate empty training VM. Give it a new virtual disk, about 30 GiB, two virtual CPUs and about 4 GiB of memory. Attach the AlmaLinux DVD as installation media. Compare its SHA-256 digest with the published checksum for that exact image. Choose the VM's language, time zone and the new virtual disk by its capacity. Select automatic partitioning and a minimal or server environment. Create `learner` as an administrator. Complete installation, eject the installation media and boot the installed disk. Perform the same three checks. If the installer starts again, inspect the boot order and the attached media.

## Leave yourself a fresh start

**Stop lab** powers down the managed pair and keeps its disks. **Reset disks** discards the shared pair's practice changes. Save any notes you want to keep outside those disks first. On a manually built kit pair, use the reference to capture its ready baseline before using the kit's reset command. For a standalone VM, take a powered-off snapshot after testing your login.

**First handoff.** Write one line for the client and one for the server giving the host name, account and distribution. Explain which machine's files would change if you typed a command at the client prompt. If your evidence says Fedora, Windows or Debian instead of AlmaLinux, pause and identify which terminal you opened.

[AlmaLinux checksums and downloads](https://almalinux.org/get-almalinux/) · [RHEL 10 documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10)

lessons.title: Read a prompt and recover from a typing mistake
lessons.body:
Open the client practice terminal and log in as your ordinary learner. In a prompt such as `[learner@client ~]$`, the text before @ is your account, the text after @ names the guest, and ~ stands for your home directory. Bash waits here for your next instruction.

Start by finding out where you are. Use a long listing to inspect the directory named /etc.

`pwd` prints the full path of the current working directory.

`ls` lists directory entries. With -l it includes permissions and ownership. Add -d to inspect the directory itself.

In the listing, the first character tells you the type of entry. Now look inside the same directory. Notice how the number of names changes.

## When a command seems to hang

Print a short message. The single quotes keep the two words together as one argument.

`printf` writes formatted text. %s inserts one argument and the backslash-n sequence ends the line.

Use the Up arrow to recall the command. Delete its closing quote and press Enter. Bash displays its own continuation prompt, usually a lone greater-than sign. It is waiting for the closing quote. Press Ctrl+C to cancel the unfinished line. Now try interrupting a running program.

`sleep` waits for the number of seconds you supply.

A waiting shell, a running program and a pager look different. Ctrl+C cancels the first two examples. In the manual-page viewer you will meet later, q closes the viewer.

## Read an error while it is fresh

Ask for a path that does not exist. Check its exit status immediately afterward.

`echo` writes its arguments followed by a newline. Bash replaces $? with the last command's exit status before echo runs.

On AlmaLinux, the missing-path listing normally returns 2. Now compare it with a successful command.

Every command replaces the previous status. If the goal is to diagnose a failed copy, read the status before running a listing or even printing a message.

**Try it independently.** Without retyping the successful listing, recall it and inspect /var. Show how you would tell the difference between a shell waiting for the rest of a quotation, a pager awaiting a key, and a command that has already failed and returned to the prompt.

lessons.title: Choose your workspace and identify both machines
lessons.body:
You are responsible for a small office's client and file server. Later a user will report a missing share, a failed login and a service that disappeared after reboot. A useful incident note starts with **where** you observed the failure and **as whom** you tested. Today you will make that baseline without changing either machine.

## Read each console

Open the shared practice terminal beside this lesson. In **Client console**, log in as `learner` using **Console login**. On a manual pair, use the account you created. Run these commands individually.

`id` shows the numeric and named identity and groups of the current user, or of the user you name.

`ip` shows and changes network settings. The address view lists addresses attached to each interface. The brief option condenses each interface into one row.

Read `uid` as the numerical identity of your account and `groups` as the memberships held by this login. `ip -brief address` lists interfaces and addresses.

Ignore `lo` for the private network comparison. The boot ID is a long identifier generated at each boot. A hostname can survive many reboots. A boot ID lets you prove that a service really worked after a restart.

Switch to **Server console** and gather the same four observations. In the supplied pair, the private server address is `192.168.77.10` and the private client address is `192.168.77.20`. Your own pair may use different addresses. Record actual values.

| Record | Client | Server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hostname and account | Fill from hostname and id | Fill from hostname and id |
| Private address and interface | Read the active interface | Read the active interface |
| Current boot | First eight characters of boot ID | First eight characters of boot ID |

## Work the course in three passes

On the first reading, predict one observable result and then run the worked example. Next, do the transfer ticket with its new filenames, accounts or values. Only then check the worked review or answer the quiz. Keep notes in your own notebook or outside the resettable guests. Use **Read your result and plan a targeted retake** after the final to choose the skill to repeat.

The shared workshop belongs to this course and learner. Navigate to another ordinary reading while it is open and check your working directory or hostname again.

A timed practical opens a different attempt. **Prepare machines** boots that attempt, and **Begin** starts its clock. Leaving a timed lesson keeps the deadline running. Stop idle pairs if your computer is short of memory. To repeat an assessment, use that practical's reset after saving any evidence you want.

**Independent handoff.** Give a partner two observations that would distinguish “wrong account,” “wrong guest,” and “right guest, different boot.” Show the command that produced each observation. A heading on the screen or a prompt by itself is weaker evidence than a command run inside the guest.

## Terminal session

Run the first four inputs on the client. Repeat them on the server starting at the second hostname check. The final working-directory check can be made from either guest.

```plaintext
>hostname
client
>id
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner),10(wheel)
>ip -brief address
lo               UNKNOWN        127.0.0.1/8 ::1/128

>cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id

>pwd
```

lessons.title: Predict what Bash will pass to a command
lessons.body:
An operator asks you to list every report in a directory. One file is named `night shift.txt`. Bash normally splits unquoted words at spaces. To see what a program actually receives, you will print each argument on its own line.

## Create a private place to practice

Read the first line from the inside out. `mktemp -d` creates a new temporary **directory** and prints its full path. Bash runs the part inside `$(...)` and substitutes that printed path. The assignment `work=` saves the path in a variable named `work`. Keep the equals sign tight against the name and value. The assignment itself prints nothing.

`mktemp` creates a uniquely named temporary file. The -d option creates a directory instead and prints its path.

Now enter that directory. In `"$work"`, the dollar sign retrieves the saved value and the quotes keep it together. Check that the working directory is the same path you just printed.

`cd` changes the current working directory of this shell. Quoting a variable keeps its path together as one argument.

## Watch where one argument ends

Create two files. The quotes around the first filename keep its space inside the name.

`touch` creates an empty file if the name is new or updates the timestamps of an existing file.

The format below puts angle brackets around each argument and starts a new line. Predict the number of lines before each command.

Two pairs of brackets mean that Bash passed two arguments. One pair around both words means it passed one. Now let Bash expand a filename pattern.

An unquoted asterisk matches names in the directory. Quoting it preserves the literal pattern. This explains how a program can receive `*.txt` even when two matching files exist.

## Store a filename for later

Set a second variable to the name with a space. Double quotes allow variable expansion. Single quotes preserve the dollar sign itself.

Bash implements some commands itself and finds others by searching the directories in PATH. Ask Bash how it resolves these two names.

`type` asks Bash how it would resolve a command name. The -a option shows every matching definition.

## Take the next ticket
Create a third file named `night cover.txt`. List just the two night filenames, one per line, then print the same wildcard literally. Arrange both results before reading on.

**Check your work.** An unquoted `night*.txt` expands to two names. Quoting that pattern produces one line containing a star. Your original directory should still contain three files. Return to your home directory with `cd`. The variable disappears when you log out, while the files remain until the temporary directory is cleaned.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>printf '%s\n' "$work"
/tmp/tmp.STm5KtzpL6
>cd "$work"

>pwd
/tmp/tmp.STm5KtzpL6
>touch 'night shift.txt' day.txt

>printf '<%s>\n' night shift.txt
<night>
<shift.txt>
>printf '<%s>\n' 'night shift.txt'
<night shift.txt>
>printf '<%s>\n' *.txt
<day.txt>
<night shift.txt>
>printf '<%s>\n' '*.txt'
<*.txt>
>ticket='night shift.txt'

>printf '<%s>\n' "$ticket"
<night shift.txt>
>printf '<%s>\n' '$ticket'
<$ticket>
>type cd
cd is a shell builtin
>type -a ls
ls is /usr/bin/ls
>touch 'night cover.txt'

>printf '%s\n' night*.txt
night cover.txt
night shift.txt
>printf '%s\n' 'night*.txt'
night*.txt
>cd

>pwd
/home/learner
```

lessons.title: Find the right manual when you forget an option
lessons.body:
A colleague asks you how to show the permissions of a directory itself. You remember `ls`, but a normal listing shows its children. An administrator needs a way to recover forgotten syntax inside the guest. Documentation is part of your working environment.

## Look up an answer, then test it

On the client, use the terminal session.

`less` opens a scrollable view. Type / followed by text to search, n for the next match, or q to quit.

The pipe feeds the help text into a pager. Type `/directory` and press Enter to search, use `n` to find the next occurrence, and press `q` to return to the shell. Now use the terminal session and find the long option `--directory`.

`man` opens an installed manual page. A section number selects a particular manual when names overlap.

Compare these observations.

`head` prints the first lines of its input. The default is ten, and -n chooses a different count.

`rpm` queries or manages RPM packages. In a query, -q selects query mode, -d selects documentation and -l lists files.

The second listing describes one directory. Its initial `d` tells you the file type. `man -w` reports where the manual comes from. `rpm -qd` lists documentation shipped by that RPM. A minimal installation may split manuals into separate packages. Use `command --help` and `ls /usr/share/doc` when a page is absent.

For Bash builtins, try `help cd` inside Bash.

`help` shows Bash's built-in documentation for a shell command such as cd.

For a GNU program with a full manual, use the terminal session, follow a menu entry with Enter and leave with `q` when Info and its manuals are installed.

`info` opens a locally installed reference manual with linked sections.

Manual section numbers distinguish different things with the same name. Compare `man 1 passwd` and `man 5 passwd`.

One describes the password-changing program. The other describes a file format. Read the heading and the synopsis before accepting an example.

## Find an unfamiliar option

Use local documentation to work out how `sort` compares numbers. Feed it the lines 12, 3 and 21. Capture the original order, the default sort and the numeric sort. Explain the difference to someone who thinks 12 is smaller than 3.

**Check your work.** `printf '%s\n' 12 3 21 | sort -n` prints 3, 12, 21.

`sort` orders the input lines. The -n option compares numeric values and -u removes duplicate lines.

Plain `sort` compares text according to the locale. Record the documentation heading and the flag that settled the question. This is the lookup routine to use in the later independent practical.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>ls --help | less
Usage: ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...
List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
>man ls
LS(1)                         User Commands                         LS(1)

NAME
       ls - list directory contents
>ls /etc | head -n 3
DIR_COLORS
DIR_COLORS.lightbgcolor
GREP_COLORS
>ls -ld /etc
drwxr-xr-x. 87 root root 8192 Nov 24 19:44 /etc
>man -w ls
/usr/share/man/man1/ls.1.gz
>rpm -qd coreutils | head

>ls /usr/share/doc
NetworkManager
attr
audit
authselect
authselect-libs
bash
c-ares
chrony
cloud-init
cloud-utils-growpart
>help cd
cd: cd [-L|[-P [-e]] [-@]] [dir]
    Change the shell working directory.

    Change the current directory to DIR.  The default DIR is the value of the
    HOME shell variable. If DIR is "-", it is converted to $OLDPWD.

    The variable CDPATH defines the search path for the directory containing
    DIR.  Alternative directory names in CDPATH are separated by a colon (:).
    A null directory name is the same as the current directory.  If DIR begins
    with a slash (/), then CDPATH is not used.
>info coreutils
File: coreutils.info,  Node: Top,  Next: Introduction,  Up: (dir)
>man 1 passwd
PASSWD(1)                         User utilities                         PASSWD(1)
>man 5 passwd
PASSWD(5)                    File Formats Manual                    PASSWD(5)
>printf '%s\n' 12 3 21
12
3

>printf '%s\n' 12 3 21 | sort
12

3
>printf '%s\n' 12 3 21 | sort -n

12
```

lessons.title: Find your way through a Linux filesystem
lessons.body:
An absolute path starts at the root directory, /. A relative path starts in the current working directory. Use the client as your ordinary learner for this exercise. The tilde in a path expands to your home directory.

## Make a work area

Create two directories for the shift, then move into their parent.

`mkdir` makes directories. With -p it also creates missing parents and accepts an existing directory.

Check where you landed and show all entries, including the special names . for this directory and .. for its parent.

Create a filename with a space and inspect it from the parent.

Change into inbox. Now try the earlier relative path again, then inspect the name relative to your new location.

## Give the next shift a copy

Copy the file into the sibling archive directory under a new name, then rename the original in inbox.

`cp` copies a file to a separate destination. The source comes first, the destination second.

`mv` renames a file or moves it to the destination in the second argument.

The archive copy has its own name and contents. Renaming the original leaves the archive name in place. Inspect the four system directories below. Configuration commonly lives under /etc, changing service data under /var, personal files under /home, and runtime state under /run. The guest recreates /run on boot.

**Independent ticket.** Put another copy of day-one into inbox under the name day-two. Remove that copy interactively and check what survived.

`rm` removes a directory entry. The -i option asks before removing each file.

`find` walks a directory tree. A test such as -type f selects ordinary files and -name restricts the filename.

The remaining files should be inbox/shift report and archive/day-one. A missing-path message is a reason to check where you started.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>mkdir -p ~/shift-practice/inbox ~/shift-practice/archive

>cd ~/shift-practice

>pwd
/home/learner/shift-practice
>ls -a
.  ..  archive	inbox
>touch 'inbox/shift notes'

>ls -l 'inbox/shift notes'
-rw-r--r--. 1 learner learner 0 Nov 24 19:44 'inbox/shift notes'
>cd inbox

>ls -l 'inbox/shift notes'
ls: cannot access 'inbox/shift notes': No such file or directory
>ls -l 'shift notes'
-rw-r--r--. 1 learner learner 0 Nov 24 19:44 'shift notes'
>cp 'shift notes' ../archive/day-one

>mv 'shift notes' 'shift report'

>ls -1 . ../archive
.:
'shift report'

../archive:
day-one
>ls -ld /etc /var /home /run
drwxr-xr-x. 87 root root 8192 Nov 24 19:43 /etc
drwxr-xr-x.  3 root root   21 Nov 24 19:43 /home
drwxr-xr-x. 33 root root  960 Nov 24 19:43 /run
drwxr-xr-x. 18 root root 4096 Nov 16 07:59 /var

>rm -i ~/shift-practice/inbox/day-two
```

lessons.title: Recover from a renamed file using links and inodes
lessons.body:
An application opens a file called `current`. An operator renames an old report, and suddenly one shortcut breaks while another still works. To predict which one, separate a directory entry (a name) from the filesystem record that holds the file's metadata and refers to its data. That record has an inode number within its filesystem.

## Change the name; observe the object

Run this in a new client practice directory. Read each listing before running the next line.

`ln` creates another name for a file. By default it creates a hard link. With -s it stores a target pathname in a symbolic link.

`readlink` prints the target text stored in a symbolic link, even if the target no longer exists.

The first two ordinary names had the same inode number and a link count of two. A hard link is another name for the same object. The symbolic link has its own inode and contains the path `original`. Renaming the target leaves that text untouched. `readlink current` can therefore succeed while `cat current` reports a missing target.

A relative target is resolved from the directory containing the symbolic link.

Write `printf 'shift 2\n' >> archived` and read `second-name`.

Both names expose the new line. Make a plain copy using `cp archived frozen`.

Append another line through `second-name`. Compare `wc -l archived second-name frozen`.

`wc` counts input. The option -l counts newline characters and -c counts bytes.

The copy stops following changes once it is made.

## Repair the handoff

Make `current` resolve to `archived` while preserving both ordinary names and the independent copy. Test the contents through each of the four names. Predict what will happen if the original directory is copied to another filesystem.

**Check your work.** Remove only your dangling symlink with `unlink current` and recreate it using `ln -s archived current`.

`unlink` removes the single directory entry named as its argument.

Run `ls -li` and `cmp archived current`.

`cmp` compares two inputs byte for byte. It is silent when they match. A dash selects standard input.

Compare inode numbers only within the same filesystem. A hard link cannot span filesystems. A symlink can span them if its target path still resolves.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>cd "$work"

>printf 'shift 1\n' > original

>ln original second-name

>ln -s original current

>ls -li
total 8
8428716 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 learner learner 8 Nov 24 19:44 current -> original
8428715 -rw-r--r--. 2 learner learner 8 Nov 24 19:44 original
8428715 -rw-r--r--. 2 learner learner 8 Nov 24 19:44 second-name
>mv original archived

>ls -li
total 8
8428715 -rw-r--r--. 2 learner learner 8 Nov 24 19:44 archived
8428716 lrwxrwxrwx. 1 learner learner 8 Nov 24 19:44 current -> original
8428715 -rw-r--r--. 2 learner learner 8 Nov 24 19:44 second-name
>cat second-name
shift 1
>readlink current
original
>cat current
cat: current: No such file or directory
>readlink current
original
>cat current
cat: current: No such file or directory
>printf 'shift 2\n' >> archived

>cat second-name
shift 1
shift 2
>cp archived frozen

>printf 'shift 3\n' >> second-name

>wc -l archived second-name frozen
 3 archived
 3 second-name
 2 frozen
 8 total
>unlink current
```

lessons.title: Edit a configuration and find help offline
lessons.body:
Many system settings are text files. An editor changes the file on disk. A service may keep using its previously loaded settings until you reload it. First practice where a typo affects only your home directory.

Run `mkdir -p ~/editor-practice` and `cd ~/editor-practice`.

Create a known starting point with `printf 'owner=morning\nqueue=1\n' > shift.conf`.

Make a backup with `cp -p shift.conf shift.conf.before`.

Open `vi shift.conf`.

`vi` opens a terminal text editor. Press i to insert text, Escape to leave insert mode and :wq followed by Enter to save and quit.

In normal mode type `/morning` and press Enter to find the word. Press `cw`, type `evening`, press Esc and type `:wq` followed by Enter. If you get lost before saving, Esc then `:q!` discards that edit. Compare files with `diff -u shift.conf.before shift.conf`.

`diff` compares files or directory trees. Use -u to see changes with surrounding lines or -r to compare subdirectories.

Lines with minus and plus show the old and new values. An exit status of one from diff means the files differ.

For a command whose options you have forgotten, ask the installed manual. Open `man cp`, search for `/preserve`, use n for the next match and q to quit.

Compare `man 1 passwd` (the program) with `man 5 passwd` (the account record format).

Use `info coreutils` where installed.

Locate package documents with `rpm -qd coreutils` and inspect `/usr/share/doc`.

A minimal image may need man-db, man-pages, info or package documentation installed from its configured source.

**Independent ticket.** Add a third line, `region=west`, without changing the first two. Show the exact change in a diff, then restore the original from your backup. Use the terminal session and inspect its status.

A silent successful comparison is a useful receipt.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>mkdir -p ~/editor-practice

>cd ~/editor-practice

>printf 'owner=morning\nqueue=1\n' > shift.conf

>cp -p shift.conf shift.conf.before

>vi shift.conf
owner=morning
queue=1
>diff -u shift.conf.before shift.conf
--- shift.conf.before   2026-11-24 08:10:00.000000000 +0000
+++ shift.conf          2026-11-24 08:11:00.000000000 +0000
@@ -1,2 +1,2 @@
-owner=morning
+owner=evening
 queue=1
>man cp
CP(1)                         User Commands                         CP(1)

NAME
       cp - copy files and directories
>man 1 passwd
PASSWD(1)                         User utilities                         PASSWD(1)
>man 5 passwd
PASSWD(5)                    File Formats Manual                    PASSWD(5)
>info coreutils
File: coreutils.info,  Node: Top,  Next: Introduction,  Up: (dir)
>rpm -qd coreutils

>vi shift.conf
owner=evening
queue=1
>diff -u shift.conf.before shift.conf
--- shift.conf.before
+++ shift.conf
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
-owner=morning
+owner=evening
 queue=1
+region=west
>cmp shift.conf.before shift.conf
shift.conf.before shift.conf differ: byte 7, line 1
>cp -p shift.conf.before shift.conf

>cmp shift.conf.before shift.conf
```

lessons.title: Follow data through a pipeline
lessons.body:
The night shift wrote four records. Your first job is to pull out the two errors and count them. Work as learner on the client. Make a fresh workspace and enter it so the example filenames are yours.

Write one record per line. Here the greater-than sign **inside** the command sends output to a file, replacing its previous contents. Keep that sign when typing.

## Search for a line with grep

`grep` compares a pattern with every input line and prints the whole line when it matches. Give it the pattern first, then the filename. The spaces inside the quoted pattern are part of the search. Predict which two records contain the word ERROR surrounded by spaces.

`grep` reads input one line at a time and prints the lines that match a pattern. Give it the pattern first and the filename second.

A pipe, written |, sends the selected lines into the next program. `wc -l` counts newline characters. Each record in this log ends with one.

The first search printed matching **records**. The pipeline prints their **count**. To find records by position, put a caret at the start of a pattern to anchor it to the beginning of a line.

The next search uses an extended regular expression. In [23], either digit can match. The dollar sign anchors the match at the end. Compare that with fixed-string mode, which searches for the brackets and dollar sign literally.

That 1 means grep successfully read the file and found zero matches. A missing input is a different problem. Try a filename absent from this new directory and read the status immediately.

## Keep the matches and the diagnostics

Save the two matching records. Run the same command a second time. A single redirection replaces the file, so there are still only two lines.

Append a review note with two greater-than signs. Read what you actually saved.

Standard output carries ordinary data. Standard error carries diagnostics. Send the two streams to different files while reading one good file and one missing file.

**Independent ticket.** Produce a file containing just the bay-2 events, in time order, and a separate count. Predict both lines before checking. Search for a bay you know is absent and immediately inspect grep's exit status. Status 1 means no match; a missing input file typically gives status 2. Decide whether each deserves the same alert.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>cd "$work"

>printf '%s\n' '08:00 OK bay-1' '08:10 ERROR bay-2' '08:20 OK bay-2' '08:30 ERROR bay-3' > shift.log

>grep ' ERROR ' shift.log
08:10 ERROR bay-2
08:30 ERROR bay-3
>grep ' ERROR ' shift.log | wc -l
2
>grep '^08:10' shift.log
08:10 ERROR bay-2
>grep -E 'bay-[23]$' shift.log
08:10 ERROR bay-2
08:20 OK bay-2
08:30 ERROR bay-3
>grep -F 'bay-[23]$' shift.log

>echo $?
1
>grep ' ERROR ' missing-file
grep: missing-file: No such file or directory
>echo $?
2
>grep ' ERROR ' shift.log > alerts

>wc -l < alerts
2
>printf '%s\n' 'manually reviewed' >> alerts

>cat alerts
08:10 ERROR bay-2
08:30 ERROR bay-3
manually reviewed
>cat shift.log missing-file > collected 2> diagnostics

>wc -l < collected
4
>cat diagnostics
cat: missing-file: No such file or directory
```

lessons.title: Read a log without counting the wrong records
lessons.body:
An overnight report needs the disk incidents from node 2. An operator searched for `disk` and counted every mention, including a recovery message. A useful search describes the exact records of interest. `grep` selects complete input lines. An extended regular expression describes their structure. A shell wildcard selects pathnames before the command runs.

## Build evidence small enough to inspect

Make a disposable directory on the client. The here-document sends the lines between two `EVENTS` markers to `cat`. Quote the first marker so the shell preserves its contents.

You should see lines 1 and 5 in the second result. The caret anchors the start. The space after `node2` prevents `node20` from matching. Parentheses group alternatives in extended mode. The final space separates the word `disk` from its message. The `-n` flag shows original line numbers, which lets a colleague reproduce your finding. Quotes make the expression one shell argument.

Use `grep -Ec '^node2 (WARN|ERROR) disk ' events` to count selected lines.

Try a search that finds nothing, then read its status immediately.

 A status of 1 means no selected lines. Try reading a missing filename and inspect its status and error message. An unreadable input and a quiet system are different conclusions. An empty output file alone cannot tell you which happened.

## Investigate another incident

Add a disk warning for node20 and an informational message for node2. Produce a report containing only node20 disk warnings and a separate file for diagnostics. Confirm the number of records and explain why an unanchored search would be risky if names/prefixes overlap.

**Check your work.** A pattern beginning `^node20 WARN disk ` matches exactly two records after your addition. Redirect selected lines with `> report` and diagnostics with `2> errors`. A successful run leaves the latter empty. Check the return status before running a different command.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>cd "$work"

>cat > events <<'EVENTS'
>node2 WARN disk busy
>node2 INFO disk recovered
>node20 WARN disk busy
>node2 WARN link down
>node2 ERROR disk offline
>EVENTS

>grep disk events
node2 WARN disk busy
node2 INFO disk recovered
node20 WARN disk busy
node2 ERROR disk offline
>grep -En '^node2 (WARN|ERROR) disk ' events
1:node2 WARN disk busy
5:node2 ERROR disk offline
>grep -Ec '^node2 (WARN|ERROR) disk ' events
2
>grep -F 'fan failure' events

>echo $?
1
```

lessons.title: Deliver a backup another operator can really restore
lessons.body:
A compressed file sitting on a disk is a promise. Test that promise by restoring the files to an empty directory and comparing their contents. An archive holds names, directory structure and metadata. Compression reduces the bytes used to store the archive. This distinction matters when deciding how to unpack a handoff.

## Build and restore a shift packet

Use the client as `learner`. `-C` gives tar a directory to work from, so the archive stores relative names that another account can restore elsewhere.

`tar` collects or extracts a tree of files. The operation c creates, t lists and x extracts. The f option takes the archive filename.

That last command deliberately selects the bzip2 decoder for a gzip file. Read the error. The source packet still exists. Use `file shift.tar.gz` if available to identify its format.

`file` inspects a file's contents and reports what type of data it recognizes.

In `-czf`, `c` creates an archive, `z` selects gzip and `f` takes the filename. Replace `c` with `t` to list it or `x` to extract it.

Both comparisons should be silent and return zero. `tar -t` verifies readable member names. `diff -r` also checks whether the restored content matches. Perform a restore into an empty destination so existing files cannot mask missing members. Inspect an archive's member list before extracting it.

## Hand off an independent restore

Add a file whose name includes a space to the source. Create a fresh archive in either format, then restore it into a third empty directory without modifying the source. Give the next operator the format, the relative member name and an observation establishing an exact restore.

**Check your work.** The member list contains the new name once. `diff -r` reports no difference, and `sha256sum` on the new source and restored file prints identical digests. Leave the two older archives intact and explain why neither contains this later file.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>cd "$work"

>mkdir -p packet/logs restore-gz restore-bz

>printf 'bay 4\n' > packet/logs/evening

>printf 'ready\n' > packet/status

>tar -czf shift.tar.gz -C packet .

>tar -tjf shift.tar.gz
bzip2: (stdin) is not a bzip2 file.
tar: Child returned status 2
tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now
>file shift.tar.gz
shift.tar.gz: gzip compressed data, from Unix, original size modulo 2^32 10240
>tar -tzf shift.tar.gz
./
./logs/
./logs/evening
./status
>tar -xzf shift.tar.gz -C restore-gz

>diff -r packet restore-gz

>tar -cjf shift.tar.bz2 -C packet .

>tar -xjf shift.tar.bz2 -C restore-bz

>diff -r packet restore-bz

>printf 'new handoff\n' > 'packet/shift note'

>mkdir restore-new

>tar -czf shift-new.tar.gz -C packet .

>tar -tzf shift-new.tar.gz
./
./logs/
./logs/evening
./status
./shift note
>tar -xzf shift-new.tar.gz -C restore-new

>diff -r packet restore-new

>sha256sum 'packet/shift note' 'restore-new/shift note'
3c8fcfa5f422d35ad0221ffe61bf1f7a9b20ab4db81ea2b78d0c21282958dbdb  packet/shift note
3c8fcfa5f422d35ad0221ffe61bf1f7a9b20ab4db81ea2b78d0c21282958dbdb  restore-new/shift note
```

lessons.title: Predict who can read, change or enter a path
lessons.body:
Linux checks the caller's identity against the file's owner, group and other permission classes. Read the first character of `ls -l` for the file type, then the three permission triplets. For a regular file, r reads data, w changes data and x permits execution. For a directory, r lists names, x traverses to a known entry, and w with x allows changes to directory entries. Deleting a file is a change to its parent directory.

Run the following as your ordinary user in an empty directory you own. The parentheses start a subshell so the changed umask lasts only for this exercise.

`umask` sets which permission bits new files and directories should lose at creation. Without an argument it displays the current mask. `stat` shows file metadata. The -c option selects fields such as %a for octal permissions or %n for the name.

`chmod` changes permissions. In symbolic modes u means owner, g group and o others. A plus grants a bit and a minus removes it.

A new ordinary file commonly starts from requested mode 666, a directory from 777. A mask of 027 removes group write and all permissions for others. Expect 640 for notes and 750 for crew. A mask removes bits from what was requested, so it cannot grant execute permission to a new ordinary file. Existing objects keep their earlier mode.

**Diagnose one failure.** Temporarily remove your own search permission with `chmod u-x crew`.

Predict whether `cat crew/notes` works.

Run it, then `namei -l "$PWD/crew/notes"` to inspect every path component.

`namei` walks a path component by component. With -l it shows the mode and owner at each step.

Restore traversal with `chmod u+x crew`.

Confirm the file is still 640. An administrator testing as root can miss this denial.

**Independent ticket.** Give the owner read/write, group read, and others no access on a second file using numeric mode. Set the parent directory so its group can enter and list it. Explain why group members who can list the filename might still fail to open the file.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>(umask 027; mkdir crew; touch crew/notes; stat -c '%a %n' crew crew/notes)
750 crew
640 crew/notes
>chmod u=rw,g=r,o= crew/notes

>ls -ld crew crew/notes
drwxr-x---. 2 learner learner 19 Nov 24 19:44 crew
-rw-r-----. 1 learner learner  0 Nov 24 19:44 crew/notes
>chmod u-x crew

>cat crew/notes
cat: crew/notes: Permission denied
>namei -l "$PWD/crew/notes"
f: /home/learner/crew/notes
dr-xr-xr-x root    root    /
drwxr-xr-x root    root    home
drwx------ learner learner learner
drw-r-x--- learner learner crew
                            notes - Permission denied
>chmod u+x crew

>stat -c '%a %n' crew/notes
640 crew/notes
```

lessons.title: Independent shift: restore an operator's handoff
lessons.body:
Your first independent assignment combines the shell, a text editor, filters, permissions and archives. Work as `learner` on the untimed client. Use local manuals freely. Read the work order before looking at the review below. The goal is to leave another operator a verifiable result. Every run starts with a new folder.

## The intake

Create an empty working directory with `mktemp -d` and save its path. In it, create a file `arrivals` containing these four lines in this order:

The receiving operator wants a directory called `handoff`. Inside it put a file `east-open` containing only open east tickets in their original order. Give the file owner read/write, group read, and others no access. Include a relative symbolic link `today` pointing to that file. Create a gzip-compressed tar archive containing the contents of `handoff`. Deliver it by restoring into a separate empty directory. Keep your original input.

## Evidence to hand back

Award yourself one check for each observable outcome: the two correct records in order, the requested file mode, a relative link that works in the restored directory, and a restore whose contents match the original. If a check fails, note the symptom and repair that part before starting over. Repeat once on fresh inputs by substituting west and CLOSED for east and OPEN. The second run is the transfer test.

## Worked review

One solution is `grep '^east OPEN ' arrivals > handoff/east-open` after creating `handoff`.

Inspect the file before setting mode 640. Run `ln -s east-open handoff/today`; constructing that target relative to the link makes the restored copy portable.

Use `tar -czf shift.tar.gz -C handoff .`, list its members, then extract with `tar -xzf shift.tar.gz -C restored` after creating `restored`.

Compare `readlink restored/today`, `stat -c '%a' restored/east-open`, `cat restored/today` and `diff -r handoff restored`.

A listing alone cannot establish that the restored symlink resolves to the right data.

## Terminal session

Try the assignment independently first. The terminal session gives one complete worked review.

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>cd "$work"

>cat > arrivals <<'ERUDIOR_FILE'
>east OPEN drive
>west CLOSED tray
>east OPEN cable
>east CLOSED drive
>ERUDIOR_FILE

>mkdir handoff restored

>grep '^east OPEN ' arrivals > handoff/east-open

>chmod 640 handoff/east-open

>ln -s east-open handoff/today

>tar -czf shift.tar.gz -C handoff .

>tar -tzf shift.tar.gz
./
./east-open
./today
>tar -xzf shift.tar.gz -C restored

>readlink restored/today
east-open
>stat -c '%a' restored/east-open
640
>cat restored/today
east OPEN drive
east OPEN cable
>diff -r handoff restored


```

lessons.title: Understand a login, a group and a privileged command
lessons.body:
A login name is the human label for a numeric user ID. Permissions use the numeric identity. A process also carries a primary group and may carry extra groups. Two machines may have the same login name and different users behind it. Start on the client and run `whoami`, `id` and `getent passwd "$(id -un)"`.

`getent` asks the configured system databases for an entry. Examples include accounts in passwd, groups in group and host addresses.

Read the account name, numeric IDs, home directory and login shell from the colon-separated account record. The x in the password field tells you that password verification data is stored separately.

List your sudo permissions and read which operations your account may request.

`sudo` runs one authorized command as another user, normally root. It may ask for your own login password.

Use `sudo id -u` if allowed.

It prints 0 when that single command runs as root. Follow it with `id -u` to see your original shell identity.

To test another account's view on your own VM, start a new login shell with `sudo -iu learner` from an authorized administrator account.

Compare `pwd`, `id` and `printf '%s\n' "$HOME"`, then `exit` to return.

`exit` leaves the current shell. In a nested shell you return to the shell that launched it.

A new shell is a separate process and inherits a set of credentials at startup.

**Worked diagnosis.** You add a person to an existing group. The account database immediately lists both groups when you run `id USERNAME`. In their open terminal, plain `id` still shows the earlier list.

Ask them to start a fresh login and repeat both checks. Changing ownership on every team file would address a different problem.

**Independent ticket.** On the client, find learner's login shell and primary group. In a fresh learner session, identify the effective user for a privileged read-only command. Record which machine answered. Explain why that result tells you nothing about who may run the same command on the server.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>whoami
learner
>id
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner),10(wheel)
>getent passwd "$(id -un)"
learner:x:1000:1000::/home/learner:/bin/bash
>sudo -l
User learner may run the following commands on client:
    (ALL) ALL
>sudo id -u
0
>id -u
1000
>sudo -iu learner

>pwd
/home/learner
>id
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner),10(wheel)
>printf '%s\n' "$HOME"
/home/learner
>exit
logout
>id
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner),10(wheel)
>id learner
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner),10(wheel)
```

lessons.title: See what changes when you become another user
lessons.body:
The same terminal can run programs with different permissions. A login session has a user ID, group IDs, a home directory and an environment. The kernel uses numeric identities to decide which operations the process may perform. A friendly name is a lookup for a number. Being allowed to use `sudo` gives you a way to request a particular privileged action.

## Observe three contexts

Use the ordinary learner account on the practice client. Start in its home directory. Write down each answer before moving on.

`sudo id` reports the identity of the child process as root when the policy allows it.

The second `whoami` still prints learner. If a password is requested, type the learner password at the console prompt. On these training guests some commands may be authorized without a password. Inspect `sudo -l` to learn which policy applies to this account.

Now use the terminal session inside the disposable guest.

Run the same identity, home and working-directory checks. A login shell normally starts in the target account's home with that account's environment. Use `exit` exactly once, then check `whoami` again.

Keep the narrowest privilege you need for the following exercises. For example, a regular user can inspect `ls -ld /etc` without privilege.

## Explain a failed write

From learner's shell, try creating a unique practice file under your own home and listing it with `ls -ln`.

Translate the numeric owner using `id -u`.

Then inspect the ownership and permissions of `/etc` without changing anything there. Explain why those two directories permit different actions. If `sudo echo text > file` fails for a privileged destination, which program tried to open the destination?

**Check your reasoning.** Bash arranges redirections before it starts `sudo`. A privileged writer such as `sudo tee` can open an approved destination itself. Save edits to real system configuration for the later lessons, where you will test the resulting settings and restore them.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>whoami
learner
>id
uid=1000(learner) gid=1000(learner) groups=1000(learner),10(wheel)
>printf '%s\n' "$HOME"
/home/learner
>pwd
/home/learner
>sudo id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
>whoami
learner
>sudo id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
>sudo -l
User learner may run the following commands on client:
    (ALL) ALL
>sudo -iu root

>whoami
root
>pwd
/root
>printf '%s\n' "$HOME"
/root
>id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
>exit
logout
>whoami
learner
>ls -ld /etc
drwxr-xr-x. 87 root root 8192 Nov 24 19:44 /etc
>ls -ln
total 0
>id -u
1000
```

lessons.title: Onboard an operator without losing existing access
lessons.body:
An operator should join a second team without losing an earlier assignment. On the untimed client, use spare names for this exercise. Check `getent passwd fieldops`, `getent group dispatch`, `getent group editors-local` and `getent group editors-night` first.

On a fresh guest the names should be unused.

`groupadd` creates a local group under the name you supply.

`useradd` creates a local account. The -m option requests a home directory and -G assigns supplementary groups.

`usermod` changes an existing account. Use -a with -G to append a group while retaining current memberships.

`chage` changes or lists password aging. The -M value sets the maximum age in days and -W sets the warning period.

Expect both supplementary groups and a 90-day maximum age. `usermod -G` replaces the supplementary list unless you append. Existing shells keep their group credentials until a new login. Set a password interactively with `sudo passwd fieldops` and verify the aging policy again.

`passwd` changes a password interactively and hides what you type.

Avoid putting passwords in shell history. To inspect the new user's login environment, use the password you just assigned. The dash starts a login shell in that user's home.

`su` opens a shell as the named account. A dash requests that account's login environment and home directory.

Rename a group with `groupmod -n NEW OLD`, lock an account with `usermod -L` and unlock it with `usermod -U`. Change a primary group with `usermod -g`; that does not touch supplementary groups.

## Rename a group and verify its identity

Record the numeric GID from `getent group editors-local`.

Run `sudo groupmod -n editors-night editors-local` and compare `getent group editors-night`, `getent group editors-local` and `id fieldops`.

`groupmod` changes a local group. With -n, give the new name first and the old name second.

Expect the same GID and the same membership under the new name. The old name should no longer resolve. What happens to a file owned by this GID?

## Delegate one administrative action

Locate `systemctl` with `command -v systemctl`.

`command` is a Bash builtin. With -v it prints the command or path the shell would use for a name.

Use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status` to grant the exact command (adjust its path if necessary).

`visudo` edits a sudo policy file with syntax checking. Use -f to select a fragment and -c to check the saved policy.

Inside visudo, enter `fieldops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl is-active chronyd.service`, save and exit.

Run `sudo visudo -c` and `sudo -l -U fieldops`.

Compare the granted command and arguments to the request. To retire only this practice identity, remove the new sudoers entry, run `sudo userdel -r fieldops`, then check that the practice groups are empty and run `sudo groupdel editors-night` and `sudo groupdel dispatch`.

`userdel` removes a local account. With -r it also removes that account's home directory.

`groupdel` removes the named local group.

Verify the lookups now return no record. A local account or group on the client has a separate database from one with the same name on the server.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>getent passwd fieldops

>getent group dispatch

>getent group editors-local

>getent group editors-night

>sudo groupadd dispatch

>sudo groupadd editors-local

>sudo useradd -m -G dispatch fieldops

>sudo usermod -aG editors-local fieldops

>id fieldops
uid=1001(fieldops) gid=1001(fieldops) groups=1001(fieldops),1002(dispatch),1003(editors-local)
>sudo chage -M 90 -W 7 fieldops

>sudo chage -l fieldops
Maximum number of days between password change          : 90
Number of days of warning before password expires        : 7
>sudo -iu fieldops id
uid=1001(fieldops) gid=1001(fieldops) groups=1001(fieldops),1002(dispatch),1003(editors-local)
>sudo passwd fieldops
Changing password for user fieldops.
New password:
Retype new password:
passwd: all authentication tokens updated successfully.
>su - fieldops
Password:
>pwd
/home/fieldops
>exit
logout
>getent group editors-local
editors-local:x:1003:fieldops
>sudo groupmod -n editors-night editors-local

>getent group editors-night
editors-night:x:1003:fieldops
>getent group editors-local

>id fieldops
uid=1001(fieldops) gid=1001(fieldops) groups=1001(fieldops),1002(dispatch),1003(editors-night)
>command -v systemctl
/usr/bin/systemctl
>sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status

>sudo visudo -c
/etc/sudoers: parsed OK
/etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status: parsed OK
>sudo -l -U fieldops
User fieldops may run the following commands on client:
    (root) /usr/bin/systemctl is-active chronyd.service
>sudo rm /etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status

>sudo visudo -c
/etc/sudoers: parsed OK
>sudo userdel -r fieldops

>sudo groupdel editors-night

>sudo groupdel dispatch


```

lessons.title: Predict who can create, read or remove a file
lessons.body:
A team member can read an existing report but cannot save a replacement. Many programs save by creating a new file and renaming it. Reading the old file and changing its parent directory require different permissions. On a directory, read lists names, execute searches through known names and write changes directory entries when traversal is allowed.

## Separate a file from its parent

Run the following as the ordinary learner on the client. `mktemp` gives this run a new disposable location.

The read succeeds. The new file fails because the directory owner has read and execute but lacks write. Restore owner write permission on the directory.

 Try `mv "$work/inbox/report" "$work/inbox/closed"`.

Renaming should now succeed, even though the file itself is read-only. Check `ls -ld` on the directory and `ls -l` on the file before explaining the result. Do these tests without `sudo` so the result reflects the learner's access.

A creation mask removes bits from the mode a program requests when creating an object. Observe it in a subshell so you can try different defaults without changing your login setup.

On this fresh directory without a default ACL, expect 640 for the file and 750 for the directory. Programs normally request 666 for ordinary files and 777 for directories. A mask of 027 clears group write and all permissions for others. Existing files keep their old modes.

## Take the access ticket

Create a second directory whose new files are readable and writable only by the owner. Have the same account create a file inside and show its numeric mode. Make the parent temporarily inaccessible for traversal, predict `cat` on the known file, then restore owner traversal and compare.

**Check your work.** `(umask 077; touch ... )` in the fresh directory produces mode 600 for an ordinary file. `namei -l` on the file path displays each directory along the way. Record the first component that stopped traversal and the single change that restored access.

lessons.title: Find evidence and build a shared directory
lessons.body:
A colleague reports that overnight copies failed. Work as learner on the untimed client. Choose an unused directory name for this run. Make a private practice directory and turn a noisy log into an archive someone else can inspect.

`install` copies files with specified permissions or creates directories when given -d. The -m option sets the mode.

Expect two errors, the same inode for the two hard-linked names, and a symbolic link containing a pathname. Rename `run.log` to `night.log`. Predict which link still reads the log, then test each. Capture the failed read with `cat run.link 2>link-error.txt`.

Restore the name and verify the symbolic link works again. Create a bzip2 version with `tar -cjf evidence.tar.bz2 run.log` after restoring the name.

Extract the archives with `tar -xzf evidence.tar.gz -C from-gzip` and `tar -xjf evidence.tar.bz2 -C from-bzip2`.

Check both restored copies with `cmp run.log from-gzip/run.log` and `cmp run.log from-bzip2/run.log`.

Both should exit zero. Look up flags using `man tar`, `info coreutils` or `/usr/share/doc`.

## A directory shared by a team

On the server, create a practice group with `sudo groupadd editors` if absent.

With `stat -c '%A %a %G' /srv/editorial` expect `drwxrws--- 2770 editors`.

Directory execute permission allows traversal. Setgid makes newly created children inherit the directory's group. It does not grant write permission by itself.

Try it with `sudo touch /srv/editorial/draft` and inspect the group on the child.

If a user cannot enter a path despite suitable final permissions, inspect every ancestor with `namei -l /srv/editorial/draft`.

In a clean practice directory, try `cp`, `mv`, a text editor, and `rm -i` on your own disposable file to practice the file lifecycle.

## Search text and redirect streams

Regular expressions select lines by pattern. `grep -E '^(ERR|WARN) ' run.log` matches lines that start with either word.

In basic syntax without `-E`, `|` and parentheses are literal characters unless escaped. Add `-v` to invert the match, `-c` to count matching lines, `-i` to ignore case and `-n` to show line numbers. Anchors `^` and `$` mark the start and end of a line.

`>` replaces a file and `>>` appends. `2>` sends standard error elsewhere. Redirections apply left to right, so `command >> all.log 2>&1` appends both streams, while `command 2>&1 >> all.log` still sends errors to the terminal. A pipe `|` connects standard output only.

To act as another user in a full login environment run `su - USER`, or `sudo -i -u USER` where sudo policy allows it. `su` without `-` keeps much of your current environment, including the working directory. Leave the other user's shell with `exit`.

## Match the quiz pattern to actual records

A caret anchors the beginning of a line. Extended mode lets parentheses group ERR and WARN, with a vertical bar meaning either one. Try records where the word also appears in the middle.

 The middle record starts with INFO. A search without the anchor would include it.

lessons.title: Follow one connection from client to service
lessons.body:
Imagine that a browser on the client asks the server for a report. It needs an address for the server, a route to that address, a listening service at a port, and permission for the traffic to reach it. Each question has a different observer. Start at the client for name and route. Inspect the server for a listener and its firewall.

An IPv4 address such as 192.168.77.20 identifies an interface on this network. The /24 prefix describes its network portion. The client can ordinarily reach 192.168.77.10 directly on the same private network. To reach a different network, it usually sends to a gateway. An IPv6 example, 2001:db8:42::20/64, uses the same address-and-prefix idea with more bits. A port identifies an application endpoint on an address. Resolving a name proves only that an address was returned.

## Draw your two machines

On each guest run `hostname` and `ip -br address`.

Label the interfaces, addresses and prefixes in a two-row table. The lo interface and 127.0.0.1 or ::1 point back to the current guest. Ask the client which path it would use with `ip route get 192.168.77.10`.

Read the device and source address. An answer to this command is the kernel's route choice; it does not send a request to the server.

On the server use the terminal session.

`ss` shows sockets. The l, n and t flags select listening TCP sockets and numeric addresses and ports.

If SSH is running, look for TCP port 22 and read the address to its left. A service bound only to 127.0.0.1 accepts local connections. A listener bound to 0.0.0.0 accepts connections addressed to any local IPv4 interface, subject to firewall and service policy.

**Independent ticket.** The file server resolves to 127.0.0.1 on the client. The server shows a healthy listener. Explain which machine the client actually contacted. Use `getent hosts` with the reported name, compare both address inventories, and describe the smallest correction. In the next lesson you will persist a hostname mapping and a separate dual-stack interface profile.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
client
>ip -br address

>ip route get 192.168.77.10
192.168.77.10 dev enp1s0 src 192.168.77.20 uid 1000
    cache
>ss -lnt
State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port Peer Address:Port
LISTEN 0      128          0.0.0.0:22        0.0.0.0:*
>getent hosts files.lab.test
127.0.0.1       files.lab.test
```

lessons.title: Read an address, a route and a connection profile
lessons.body:
Your client and server live on one virtual Ethernet link. An interface is the guest's endpoint on that link. An IP address identifies a destination at the network layer. A prefix marks the shared network portion of an address. On the lab's IPv4 `/24`, the first 24 bits (the first three octets) identify the network. The client at `192.168.77.20` and the server at `192.168.77.10` therefore share a subnet. A default gateway matters when no more specific route matches.

## Predict the path before sending a packet

Use the client console. A loopback address, such as `127.0.0.1` or `::1`, sends traffic back to this guest. Find the other interface carrying the client lab address.

`nmcli` reads or changes NetworkManager settings. A device is a live interface and a connection is a saved configuration profile.

Read the `dev` and `src` fields from the route lookup. They identify the outgoing interface and chosen source. A peer on the directly attached prefix generally needs no router. Compare the interface name with the active NetworkManager profile on that device. A device can be called `enp1s0` while its saved profile has a descriptive name. Record the actual values from your guest. A lab without an external default route can still reach its private peer.

IPv6 also uses prefixes. A `/64` leaves 64 bits for the interface identifier. A short address containing `::` omits a run of zero groups. Link-local addresses beginning with `fe80:` apply to one link, so an interface matters when choosing their scope. Use `ip -6 address show` and `ip -6 route show` to inspect the available IPv6 information.

The following lesson creates a dummy interface so you can configure IPv4 and IPv6 without changing the connection to the lab server.

## Trace a report from the right guest

Without changing either machine, find the route back to the client from the server. Then compare `getent hosts localhost` on the two guests and explain why the results alone cannot identify the other machine.

Use `ping -c 2 192.168.77.10` on the client if the network permits ICMP.

`ping` sends echo requests to test reachability. The -c option limits the number of requests.

A failed ping alone does not establish that an application port is closed.

**Check your work.** The peer-facing source on the server is .10 and on the client is .20. A correct handoff names the source, destination and interface for each direction and distinguishes a live route from a saved connection profile.

lessons.body:

On the server inspect listening TCP sockets with `ss -lnt`.

A resolver failure, missing route and closed listener have different remedies.

Add `192.168.77.10 server.workshop.test` once to the client's `/etc/hosts`, then use the terminal session.

`awk` processes input one record at a time. Its $1, $2 and later fields select individual columns.

Expect one unique address. Multiple rows for stream and datagram socket types are normal. Check `grep '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf` to see where applications look up hosts.

`dig` queries DNS directly and may miss a valid local hosts entry.

## Configure a practice interface without changing the lab link

In the untimed client with NetworkManager available, create a dummy profile. Check that `workshop-dummy` and `dummy42` are unused first.

Verify both addresses and the autoconnect setting. Reboot the workshop guest and verify again. Keep the profile for the next exercise. Keep the engine-provided interface unchanged. A connection profile persists configuration; commands such as `ip addr add` change runtime state.

## Change an existing profile and the hostname

Tasks usually modify the profile that already exists for an interface. Find it with `nmcli connection show` and `nmcli device status`.

Practice on the dummy profile before you remove it:

`+` adds to a list property instead of replacing it. A change to a profile takes effect when the connection is activated again. Profiles are stored as keyfiles under `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections`; `nmtui` edits the same profiles interactively. The saved profile’s ipv4.dns field holds its DNS server addresses. Reactivate the profile after updating it so the new values become active. NetworkManager writes `/etc/resolv.conf` from active profiles, so DNS servers belong in the profile rather than a hand edit of that file.

Set a persistent static hostname with `sudo hostnamectl set-hostname NAME` and check it with `hostnamectl` and a new login.

`hostnamectl` reports system identity and manages the saved hostname. The --static option prints just the configured name.

The `hostname` command alone changes only the running system. Restore the guest's original hostname when you finish, because the course uses it to tell the guests apart.

When both addresses have been verified, remove only the dummy profile using `sudo nmcli connection delete workshop-dummy`.

Verify the private lab route with `ip route get 192.168.77.10`.

lessons.title: Follow software from a trusted source to an installed file
lessons.body:
A user asks for the program that inspects a directory tree. Your system can answer three different questions. The shell can locate an executable on its search path. The RPM database can tell you which installed package owns a file. DNF can query available repositories to find software even before installation. A successful repository listing alone installs nothing.

Run `command -v bash`, `rpm -q bash` and `rpm -ql bash | head`.

Write one sentence for each result. Compare `rpm -q tree` with `dnf info tree` on an AlmaLinux guest with BaseOS and AppStream enabled.

`dnf` looks up and installs RPM packages using configured repositories. Read its proposed transaction before confirming it.

DNF might show a candidate version while RPM reports no installed package. If DNF cannot find metadata, inspect `dnf repolist --enabled`, the source URL and whether that AlmaLinux guest can reach its mirror or has matching installation media attached.

## Observe a transaction

On your disposable guest with a working source, select a small optional package that is not already installed, such as tree. Use the terminal session.

Read the transaction summary before accepting. Check `rpm -q tree`, run `tree --version`, and ask `rpm -qf "$(command -v tree)"` which package supplied it.

`tree` displays a directory and its children as a tree. The -L option limits the number of levels.

Try `dnf check-update tree`; status 100 means updates are available.

When a newer build exists, apply `sudo dnf upgrade tree` and compare versions.

Use `sudo dnf remove tree` to retire your practice installation and inspect the removal summary before confirming.

Restore the previous state if you started with a different package.

AlmaLinux uses distribution mirrors. Red Hat’s CDN serves signed RHEL packages to a registered, entitled RHEL machine. Practice the RHEL-specific registration steps in the manual-pair reference if you have access to RHEL. An internal RPM repository can use an approved HTTPS URL. The repository root must contain its repodata directory. A local RPM file also needs trusted signing keys and available dependencies. A Flatpak remote distributes applications and runtimes separately from the host RPM database. User-scope commands act for the account that runs them.

lessons.title: Choose and verify a software source
lessons.body:
A branch office receives software over removable media. DNF needs a repository root containing `repodata/repomd.xml`. The URL refers to that root. A repository ID identifies the entry to DNF, while `name` is a human-readable label.

## Inspect a local repository

`test` evaluates a condition through its exit status. For example, -r checks readability and ! reverses the test.

Metadata refresh should succeed even though the shelf has no application packages. For a local RPM, obtain the expected signing key and its fingerprint from the trusted publisher. On a guest with the verified key in its RPM keyring use the terminal session on the actual file.

Look for an OK signature from the expected key. Digests alone establish file integrity. Install with `sudo dnf --setopt=localpkg_gpgcheck=1 install ./package.rpm` to enforce local-file signature checks.

Trusted repositories must supply any dependencies. Use `rpm -q NAME` to verify the installed version. On AlmaLinux, query the enabled sources with `dnf repolist` and update a practice package with `sudo dnf upgrade NAME` when a newer build exists.

Review the transaction before removing a package you added with `sudo dnf remove NAME`.

For a network repository, obtain an approved HTTPS repository root and its key file. Create a separate [workshop-net] section with this baseurl, enabled=1, gpgcheck=1 and gpgkey pointing to the approved key. Test `sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=workshop-net makecache` and query a package available in that source.

## Self-check with a Flatpak remote

Choose an unused remote name (training below) and an app absent from this account. Use the terminal session with the actual descriptor.

Keep existing apps, runtimes and remotes.

On an Internet-connected disposable guest where Flathub is approved, the remote-add step can use `flatpak remote-add --user training https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo`.

A disconnected guest needs a supplied remote with accessible app and runtime content.

Without `--user`, `flatpak remote-add` and `flatpak install` act on the system-wide installation and need administrative rights. Read the task for which scope it wants, then verify with `flatpak remotes` and `flatpak list --app` (system) or the same commands with `--user`. 

On the disconnected course pair, continue to **Install from a signed Flatpak remote without Internet access** for a complete exercise with its own local source and public key.

lessons.title: Install from a signed Flatpak remote without Internet access
lessons.body:
A desktop app can be installed for just one account. Flatpak keeps that account's remotes and installed references in a different installation from the system-wide one. A remote supplies a catalog and signed objects. An application can depend on a runtime. Removing an application does not necessarily remove its runtime.

## Stock the practice shelf

On the untimed client, open **Make the offline Flatpak practice shelf** in this lesson's references. Run its setup once as learner. It creates a tiny local repository, two signed references and a public key under `~/rhcsa-flatpak-shelf`. You are acting as both publisher and consumer inside a disposable guest. The sample application contains an inventory document. The exercise assesses installation, scope and removal. For a real publisher, verify its key through a separately trusted source.

## Perform the request as the learner

First check `flatpak remotes --user` and `flatpak list --user`.

Continue with an unused remote name and a fresh copy of the lab where the two exercise IDs are absent. The following commands register the shelf and inspect what it offers. Import only the **public** key.

Review the proposed app and runtime during installation. If Flatpak asks where to get the runtime, choose the local shift-shelf. `flatpak info` identifies the origin. Find the payload with `flatpak info --user --show-location org.erudior.ShelfNotes` and read `files/share/inventory.txt` inside that deployment.

A user installation is meaningful even on a machine without a graphical session.

## Prove removal without disturbing other software

Retire the app, its course-only runtime and this remote. In this fresh exercise use `flatpak uninstall --user org.erudior.ShelfNotes`, then `flatpak uninstall --user org.erudior.ShelfPlatform`, then `flatpak remote-delete --user shift-shelf`.

Compare the before and after lists with the original baseline. Keep the shelf itself so you can repeat under a different remote name.

**Check your work.** A complete handoff shows the trusted source in the user installation, the installed app's ID and origin, the inventory text and the post-removal lists. lessons.title: Tell a process, a shell job and a service apart
lessons.body:
When you launch a command, the kernel gives its process a numeric ID (PID). A shell can keep track of jobs it started. A service manager can start and supervise processes even after an administrator logs out. These are three views of running work. Killing a process belonging to a service can trigger its restart policy.

## Watch one harmless process

Start `sleep 120 &` as your regular user.

The ampersand returns control of the terminal immediately. Save its PID with `worker=$!`, then run `jobs -l` and `ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,ni,comm -p "$worker"`.

`jobs` lists the background jobs launched by the current interactive shell.

`ps` shows process information. The -p option selects a PID and -o chooses which fields to show.

The parent PID identifies the process that launched it. A sleeping process usually consumes almost no CPU. Use `top`, press P to sort by CPU or M for memory, then q to exit.

`top` opens a live process display. Use q to return to the shell.

Compare a process's resident memory with the system view in `free -h`.

`free` shows memory and swap usage. The -h option formats sizes in readable units.

Linux uses spare memory as cache; the available column includes memory it can make available to programs.

Open another terminal as the same user. Its `jobs` list does not show the first shell's job, while `ps -p PID` with the recorded number can still see it.

Back in the original shell, check the PID still identifies your sleep process, then use the terminal session.

`kill` sends a signal to a process identified by its PID. TERM requests orderly termination.

Use `wait "$worker"` followed by `ps -p "$worker"` to observe completion.

`wait` waits for a child of this shell and returns that child's termination status.

TERM requests termination and allows a program to clean up. Select a specific disposable process for this exercise.

**Independent ticket.** A dashboard lists two processes with the same name. Show how to distinguish them using PID, owner and parent. Before adjusting priority, decide whether the symptom is CPU contention or a process waiting for I/O. In the next exercise, predict the direction of a nice-value change before you apply it.

lessons.title: Distinguish a busy CPU from memory pressure
lessons.body:
“The server feels slow” is a symptom. Before stopping a process, find out which resource is under pressure, which process owns it and over what interval the evidence was collected. A process is one running instance of a program. Its PID distinguishes that instance from another copy with the same name.

## Read three different observations

In the client run `uptime`, `free -h` and `ps -eo pid,user,stat,pcpu,pmem,comm --sort=-pcpu | head`.

`uptime` shows how long the guest has run and its recent load averages.

Load averages summarize runnable work and certain waiting tasks over time. CPU utilization reports time spent doing work. In `free`, read the **available** column as well as **free**. Linux can reclaim some cached memory. Little unused RAM by itself does not prove an application needs to be killed.

Start a short-lived job you own. A background command returns the prompt. `$!` is the PID Bash recorded for that command.

`renice` changes the scheduling nice value of an existing process. A larger value gives it lower priority under CPU contention.

A sleeping process is normally in state S and consumes little CPU. Its parent PID identifies the shell that launched it. Increasing the numeric nice value gives other normal work more preference when the CPU is contested. It does not guarantee a percentage. A nonzero status from `wait` after a deliberate signal is expected. Recheck the saved PID immediately to see that this job has exited.

## Make a defensible incident note

Open `top`, observe two refreshes and exit with `q`.

Compare the memory leader with the CPU leader using `ps` sorted separately by `-pmem` and `-pcpu`. Report PID, owner, command and sampling method. If the rankings change between samples, say so. Explain why a high CPU reading from the workload you intentionally launched would lead to a different action from the same reading on a shared service.

**Check your work.** Your report identifies an instance and an observation interval. You should be able to explain why the sleeping training process could have a large elapsed time and virtually no CPU use at the same time.

lessons.title: Follow a slowdown from process to journal
lessons.body:
A server is sluggish after a scheduled job. Start with evidence from the current boot. On the workshop server, run `uptime`, `free -h` and `ps -eo pid,user,ni,pcpu,pmem,comm --sort=-pcpu | head`.

Reorder by `-pmem` to find memory consumers. Load, CPU use and memory pressure answer different questions. `top` shows the same ranking live; press `P` or `M` to sort, `k` to signal a process and `q` to quit.

`pkill -u USER NAME` and `kill PID` send TERM by default. Use `kill -KILL` only after TERM has had a chance, because the process cannot clean up.

## Follow one process you own

`nice` starts a program with an adjusted scheduling priority.

Use a shell starting at nice value 0. The initial +5 is relative to the shell. If ps races the launch, repeat it once sleep appears. Expect nice 5, then 10 after renice. Bash wait normally returns 143 when TERM ends the sleep. A higher nice number gives a normal process a lower scheduling priority. Diagnose a service with `systemctl status NAME` and `journalctl -b -u NAME`, replacing NAME with the unit. Record the first failure and its timestamp. To preserve messages on a default journald setup using `Storage=auto`, create `/var/log/journal` with sudo, run `sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal` then `sudo journalctl --flush`.

`systemd-tmpfiles` creates or maintains filesystem objects according to system configuration rules.

`journalctl` reads systemd's journal. Use -b to select a boot and -u to select a unit.

If policy explicitly sets volatile storage, configure `Storage=persistent` in a journald drop-in and restart journald. Write `logger -t workshop-boot 'workshop boot evidence'`.

`logger` sends a message to the system log. The -t option gives the message a searchable tag.

After a planned workshop reboot check `sudo journalctl -b -1 -t workshop-boot` or search the previous boot by message.

## Choose a tuning profile

Run `tuned-adm list`, `tuned-adm recommend` and `tuned-adm active`.

`tuned-adm` inspects and selects system performance profiles managed by TuneD.

Record the current profile name before changing it. On the workshop server choose an installed profile such as `balanced` with `sudo tuned-adm profile balanced`.

Verify with `tuned-adm active` and `sudo tuned-adm verify`.

Explain why maximizing throughput and reducing energy use can favor different settings. Restore the prior profile when finished.
