lessons.title: Read a failure in the journal and preserve its evidence
lessons.body:
The first useful error often appears several lines before a final “failed” status. The journal records the unit, boot, timestamp and message. Choose the scope before drawing a conclusion. If a request failed after a reboot, the current boot may be healthy while yesterday's evidence has gone.

On your disposable system, choose a new unique name, for example `unit=shift-check-$(date +%s)`.

`date` prints a time using the selected format and time zone. The +%s format produces seconds since the Unix epoch.

Use `sudo systemd-run --unit="$unit" /usr/bin/false`.

`systemd-run` asks systemd to start a temporary unit for the supplied command.

This asks systemd to run a temporary service whose program deliberately exits with status 1. The launcher may report that it scheduled the unit successfully. Run `sudo systemctl status "$unit.service" --no-pager` and `sudo journalctl -b -u "$unit.service" --no-pager`.

`systemctl` talks to systemd. It can inspect a service, start it now or enable it for future boots.

Identify the executable, the exit status and the subsequent unit failure. The launch request and the program's outcome are separate events.

Compare `journalctl --list-boots`, `journalctl -b -p warning` and `sudo journalctl --since '10 minutes ago'`.

Set up persistent storage and flush the journal as described in the previous workshop. Run `logger -t shift-handoff 'dispatch verified'` and look it up with `sudo journalctl -b -t shift-handoff`.

Use the terminal session and reboot your disposable guest.

On the new boot, search `sudo journalctl -b -1 -t shift-handoff`.

If boot -1 is unavailable, check the configured Storage setting and whether a persistent journal directory exists. Write a fresh marker and repeat after changing the setting.

**Independent ticket.** A manager asks for proof that the failed service ran on the *prior* boot. Supply its unit name, the earlier boot ID, one diagnostic line and its exit status. Explain why an old log line from a different boot could lead the next shift to change a healthy service.

lessons.title: Make a service leave evidence on every boot
lessons.body:
A service can be running now and absent after reboot. It can also be enabled and failing on every start. Use a practice oneshot unit to observe what each state means. On the workshop server save the following in `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-stamp.service`.

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, then `sudo systemctl start workshop-stamp`.

Confirm the boot ID changed. Inspect `stat /run/workshop-stamp` and `sudo journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`.

The guest recreated /run at startup, so a marker on the new boot is evidence of a fresh invocation.

Self-check: stop the practice unit and predict both state queries before running them. Start it again and inspect `systemctl cat workshop-stamp` and `journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`.

lessons.title: Repair a boot job that only root can run
lessons.body:
Dispatch receives a small boot-time job. Root can read its configuration at the console, yet systemd reports that the job failed. Your job is to explain the discrepancy, make the smallest repair, and verify the result after reboot.

Use the **untimed practice server**. The marker in this exercise is public training text. The permission fault is deliberate. Leave the practice client available for reading or notes. First check `getent passwd erushift`, `getent group erushift`, `systemctl cat erudior-shift-read.service` and `sudo ls -ld /etc/erudior-shift-read`.

Start with unused names on a new pair or continue with the objects you created for this exercise.

## Install the job and observe the failure

On a fresh server, create a service identity and its configuration. The directory lets the group traverse it. The file initially allows only root to read it.

`tee` writes its input both to a file and to standard output. Run it with sudo when opening the destination needs privilege.

`chown` sets the user and group that own a file. A colon separates owner and group in the argument.

`restorecon` applies the SELinux label defined by policy for each specified path.

Expect the last command to fail. Find the denial in `sudo journalctl -b -u erudior-shift-read.service --no-pager`.

Which account opened the file? Compare the unit's effective identity, the two modes and an actual read as that identity.

The root read succeeds and the service read fails. The process needs search permission on every parent and read permission on the file. It has the former. Predict the single mode bit that will fix the latter while keeping the marker private to root and the service group.

## Repair and prove the boot result

A successful oneshot can be **inactive** after completing its work. Expect Result=success, ExecMainStatus=0 and an exact shift=evening message. Earlier failures can still appear in this boot's journal. Record the boot ID and use the terminal session on the practice server.

Reconnect and run these checks before starting the unit yourself.

## Independent repair

A second ticket arrives. Set `sudo chmod 0740 /etc/erudior-shift-read` and start the unit again.

The file still has mode 0640. Show that root can read it, the configured identity cannot, and the nonzero service exit matches the journal. Repair the parent with the smallest change that restores traversal to erushift. Restart the job. Give the next operator the two final modes, the successful service result and the outsider's failed read. Award yourself the handoff only if all three are present.

To check your diagnosis, the expected modes are 0750 for the directory and 0640 for the file. Group read on a directory allows listing names. Group execute allows looking up the named file. Keep the service running as erushift and SELinux enforcing throughout.

lessons.title: Choose when a job should run and how to prove it ran
lessons.body:
A storage report is needed once after tonight’s maintenance, a second report is needed every weekday morning, and a third should catch up if the machine was off at its scheduled time. Write the three requirements as promises. The mechanism follows from the promise. An at job leaves the queue after it executes. A cron entry describes matching wall-clock minutes. A systemd calendar timer can trigger a paired service and can catch up on a missed event when Persistent=true.

Read `timedatectl` on the guest.

`timedatectl` shows the system clock, time zone and time synchronization settings.

Which time zone is in effect? A schedule for 08:00 on a server set to UTC is a different promise from 08:00 local office time. A correctly formatted date can still be wrong if the clock is drifting. Use `chronyc tracking` and `chronyc sources -v` when chronyd is installed.

`chronyc` asks chronyd about its time sources and synchronization state.

A selected upstream and a recent useful update are better evidence than a running process alone.

## Work it out before editing

Interpret `15 6 * * 1-5` from left to right as minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. On a normally configured cron host this matches weekdays at 06:15 in its scheduling time zone. A user's crontab has five time fields followed by its command. System crontab entries include a username field. Adding that field to a per-user crontab makes cron try to execute that word as a command.

**Independent ticket.** Put the guest's time zone, intended local time and expected next run in your notes. In the following workshop schedule a timestamp into a practice log. Find evidence at three places: the configured schedule, the scheduler's decision, and the output produced by the job. If the job works in your terminal only, compare the command's path, user, working directory and output redirection.

lessons.title: Build a scheduled service and prove it actually ran
lessons.body:
A nightly backup ticket has two separate promises: a scheduler will request work, and the work will succeed. A systemd timer represents the first. Its associated service represents the second. Checking only the next firing time leaves half the ticket untested.

## Run the work before scheduling it

Use the untimed client's **system** manager. Check `systemctl cat rhcsa-stamp.service rhcsa-stamp.timer` first.

Use these names only if they are unused. In `/etc/systemd/system/rhcsa-stamp.service` write the service definition shown in the transcript.

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo systemctl start rhcsa-stamp.service`.

The date written to standard output goes to the journal. Inspect `journalctl -u rhcsa-stamp.service -n 8` with sudo if needed.

A successful oneshot may already be inactive. `systemctl show rhcsa-stamp.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus` reports the last execution.

## Schedule it and inspect both pieces

Create `/etc/systemd/system/rhcsa-stamp.timer`:

The matching unit names connect the timer to the service. Validate the expression with `systemd-analyze calendar '*-*-* 06:15:00'` and read the next date in the guest's local zone.

`systemd-analyze` inspects systemd behavior. Its calendar command parses a schedule and predicts the next firing.

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo systemctl enable --now rhcsa-stamp.timer`.

Check `systemctl list-timers --all rhcsa-stamp.timer`.

A persistent calendar timer can catch up when it becomes active after a missed firing. It does not repair a failing service.

## Deliver a schedule change

Change the timer to 17:40 on weekdays. Prove the next firing is a weekday, the timer is enabled for startup, and the underlying task still produces a timestamp. For a short live test, temporarily set `OnCalendar=minutely`, reload and restart the timer, then wait for the journal to gain a new entry without manually starting the service. Restore your weekday schedule.

**Check your work.** `Mon..Fri *-*-* 17:40:00` is one valid calendar expression. Record both the next firing and the most recent service result. To retire the exercise, disable and stop your timer, remove only these two practice unit files and reload the manager.

The job leaves the queue after execution; check the actual log. For recurring work in an image with cronie and active crond, use `crontab -e` and add `*/2 * * * * /usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-cron.log`.

`crontab` manages the current user's recurring schedule. Use -e to edit it and -l to list it.

lessons.title: Decide whether a server's clock can be trusted
lessons.body:
A report from two machines seems to describe events in the wrong order. The system clock represents an instant. The time zone controls how that instant is displayed. Clock synchronization disciplines the clock against a selected source. Changing the display zone can make a timestamp look familiar while leaving the two machines just as far apart.

## Read the same instant two ways

On the untimed client compare `date --iso-8601=seconds` with `date -u --iso-8601=seconds`.

The zone offsets may differ. Try `TZ=America/Denver date --iso-8601=seconds`.

This sets the environment for one command and leaves the machine's configured time zone untouched. On both guests, collect the time settings, service status and chrony measurements.

A running daemon can still lack a usable time source. In the source list, `^` identifies a server source and `*` marks the selected source. A `?` indicates an unusable or as-yet-unmeasured source. Check reachability, synchronization state and elapsed time since startup. On an isolated lab, an unreachable Internet pool is a valid observation. It does not establish synchronization. Use UTC when comparing journal entries across machines.

## Configure a client against a supplied source

On the practice client, first establish the address of an approved reachable NTP server. For an offline pair, use the local chrony server setup in **Build your own client and server**. Verify the server allows the lab subnet and its firewall permits the NTP service there. Keep a copy of the client's `/etc/chrony.conf`. Add a single `server 192.168.77.10 iburst` directive when .10 is that prepared source. Restart `chronyd`, wait for polling and compare `chronyc sources -n` with `chronyc tracking`.

If several sources are usable, chrony may select a different one. Report what the selection marker says. Restore your original configuration after the exercise.

## Decide whether to close the ticket

One guest reports `active` and all sources `^?`. The other reports a selected source and a recent reference time. Which evidence would you request before claiming the first system has reliable time? Translate a journal record to UTC and compare it against the other guest.

**Check your work.** Give the source address, selection state, reach field and last reference time, plus one timestamp from `journalctl --utc -n 1`.

A private server using chrony's local reference is useful for practicing the protocol. It does not establish the accuracy of that server's clock against an external standard.

lessons.title: Lab • Restore a startup service
lessons.body:
On the **server**, the supplied `erudior-maint.service` creates a runtime marker. Start it now and enable it for future boots. Inspect the supplied unit before you change its state.

Use two systemctl queries to verify active and enabled independently. Then inspect `/run/erudior-maint.ready` and the unit's journal. If it is active but disabled, decide what the next reboot would do. If it is enabled but failed, read the first error in the current boot. Leave the supplied unit performing its original job and submit for the reboot check.

## Reason through a reported result

Immediately after enabling a unit it still reports inactive. How can both observations be true?

**Check your reasoning.** Enablement connects the unit to a future startup target. Inspect the live status and use the expected runtime marker to distinguish starting now from enabling for boot.

lessons.title: Lab • Schedule a recurring job
lessons.body:
On the **client**, add an entry to the `learner` account's own crontab that runs `logger erudior-nightly` every day at 02:15.

In a learner login on the client, open the user’s crontab. The five time fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week.

From a root console, select the learner account explicitly when editing its table.

Back in the learner login, verify the saved line and check that the scheduler runs now and at boot.

To test delivery now, add a temporary entry for the next minute, wait for it to run, and read the journal on the client.

Remove the temporary entry after testing. Keep the daily entry.

The grader reads learner's crontab and checks the daily 02:15 entry and the daemon, before and after a client reboot. Entries in `/etc/crontab` or `/etc/cron.d` do not count for this task, because it asks for the user's own table.

## Terminal session

Choose the editor invocation for your current identity. As learner, use the first. As root, use the second to edit learner’s schedule. Use the remaining checks after the entry has been saved.

```plaintext
>crontab -e
crontab: installing new crontab
>crontab -u learner -e

>crontab -l
```

lessons.title: Independent shift: diagnose a service that missed its schedule
lessons.body:
A branch office wants an audit timestamp once per hour. Another operator enabled a timer, saw a next run, and marked the request complete. The handoff folder is empty. Your job is to reproduce the failure, narrow it to one layer, repair it and leave evidence that the next operator can repeat. Use a disposable untimed client with the timer workshop completed or use fresh unit names.

## Build the incident on your training client

Using the paired-unit design from the timer workshop, create `rhcsa-audit.service` and `rhcsa-audit.timer`. Use `OnCalendar=hourly` for the timer and `WantedBy=timers.target`. In the oneshot service use `ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch /run/rhcsa-shift-audit/delivered`. Start with `/run/rhcsa-shift-audit` absent and ensure both names are unused. Set up and enable the timer. Trigger the service manually once to gather evidence now. Write down the exact command that failed and the relevant journal message.

## Repair the actual cause

The configuration must recreate its required runtime directory on every service activation, leave the marker visible after a successful run, and schedule future work across boot. The filesystem under `/run` is temporary. Creating the directory manually once can hide the defect until the next boot. Find a service configuration or a preparation action that meets these conditions. Avoid changing unrelated permissions on /run.

Award one check each for a recorded initial failure, a successful manual service run, an enabled timer with a plausible next firing, and a repeated successful trigger after reboot. Wait for both practice machines to return. Record the new boot ID. A missing marker immediately after boot is expected if no scheduled activation has occurred yet. Prove what happens when the service actually runs.

## Worked review

One solution adds `ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/mkdir -p /run/rhcsa-shift-audit` in the service's `[Service]` section. The manager runs it before the existing `ExecStart`. Reload the units, start the service and compare the marker's modification time with the journal. Review `systemctl show rhcsa-audit.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus`.

Query `is-enabled` and `list-timers` for the timer. Repeat after reboot. Disable and stop the training timer and remove only its two practice units when you finish.

```plaintext
>sudoedit /etc/systemd/system/rhcsa-audit.service

>sudo systemctl daemon-reload

>sudo systemctl restart rhcsa-audit.service

>systemctl show rhcsa-audit.service -p Result -p ExecMainStatus
Result=success
ExecMainStatus=0
>systemctl is-enabled rhcsa-audit.timer
enabled
>systemctl list-timers --all rhcsa-audit.timer
NEXT                        LEFT LAST PASSED UNIT              ACTIVATES
Tue 2026-11-24 09:00:00 UTC  50m -    -      rhcsa-audit.timer rhcsa-audit.service
>sudo systemctl reboot

>sudo systemctl start rhcsa-audit.service

>stat -c "%n" /run/rhcsa-shift-audit/delivered
/run/rhcsa-shift-audit/delivered
```

lessons.title: Build a decision from arguments and exit statuses
lessons.body:
A script is a saved series of shell instructions. Its caller needs to know what to pass in, what output to expect and how failure is reported. Start with an ordinary task: label a shipment as small or bulk. For this exercise enter one to four ASCII digits for a package count between 0 and 9999. Leading zeroes are allowed. Writing down the contract lets you decide what to do with 9, 10, an empty input and the word ten.

Save the following in a fresh file called shipment. Inspect the first line before running it.

The first line selects the interpreter. The shell supplies the number of arguments in `$#` and the first argument in `$1`. The test command inside brackets returns an exit status that if uses to choose a branch. Leave spaces around its words. Use the terminal session.

Then run `./shipment 9`, `./shipment 10`, `./shipment 0009`, `./shipment 9999`, `./shipment 10000`, `./shipment ten` and `./shipment`.

Inspect `echo $?` directly after each.

The invalid cases should write a diagnostic and exit 2. The threshold itself belongs in the upper group.

**Independent ticket.** Change the boundary to 25 and process three separate counts without editing the script again. Try `for count in 24 25 26; do ./shipment "$count"; done`.

Explain what varies on each iteration and what stays fixed. In the next workshop you will preserve multiple input filenames, including names with spaces, and capture the output of another command inside the script.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>cat > shipment <<'ERUDIOR_FILE'
>#!/bin/sh
>if [ "$#" -ne 1 ]; then
>    echo 'give one package count' >&2
>    exit 2
>fi
>case "$1" in
>    ''|*[!0-9]*|?????*) echo 'use one to four digits' >&2; exit 2 ;;
>esac
>if [ "$1" -lt 10 ]; then
>    echo small
>else
>    echo bulk
>fi
>ERUDIOR_FILE

>head -n 1 shipment
#!/bin/sh
>chmod u+x shipment

>./shipment 9
small
>./shipment 10
bulk
>./shipment 0009
small
>./shipment 9999
bulk
>./shipment 10000
use one to four digits
>./shipment ten
use one to four digits
>./shipment
give one package count
>echo $?
2
>for count in 24 25 26; do ./shipment "$count"; done
small
bulk
bulk
```

lessons.title: Turn a shell command into a testable tool
lessons.body:
The next shift needs a tool that can report on several files without losing a filename that contains spaces. A script has a contract. Specify its arguments, output, exit status and required permissions before you write it.

In your home directory, save this as `line-report`. The first line selects the interpreter when the file is executed directly. Quotes around `"$@"` preserve the original arguments individually.

Create a file containing two newline-terminated lines named `shift notes`. Use the terminal session and check for `2 shift notes`.

Run `./line-report missing >out.txt 2>err.txt`, immediately check `echo $?`, and inspect both files.

An error belongs on standard error so the next program can use standard output as data.

## Try a numeric boundary

Make a second executable that reads its first argument as a number and prints `low` below 5 and `high` otherwise. Use the shell numeric test `[ "$1" -lt 5 ]`, leaving spaces around the bracket tokens. Exercise 0, 4, 5 and 17. Try launching the installed script by its full path as a second user. A script that works only when invoked with `bash scriptname` may have a bad shebang or lack execute permission.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>cd

>cat > line-report <<'ERUDIOR_FILE'
>#!/bin/sh
>if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
>    printf '%s\n' 'supply at least one file' >&2
>    exit 2
>fi
>for file in "$@"; do
>    if [ -f "$file" ] && [ -r "$file" ]; then
>        lines=$(wc -l < "$file") || exit 1
>        printf '%s %s\n' "$lines" "$file"
>    else
>        printf 'unreadable: %s\n' "$file" >&2
>        exit 1
>    fi
>done
>ERUDIOR_FILE

>chmod 755 line-report

>printf '%s\n' first second > 'shift notes'

>./line-report 'shift notes'
2 shift notes
>./line-report missing >out.txt 2>err.txt

>echo $?
1
>cat out.txt

>cat err.txt
unreadable: missing
```

lessons.title: Write a read-only inventory script and test its contract
lessons.body:
Night shift needs a list of the files that exist and the paths that were missing. An operator must be able to pass several paths, including one with a space, and use the exit status in a second script. Start by specifying what success and failure mean. A command can print something plausible while still handling an edge case incorrectly.

## Build one small program

Create a fresh directory in the learner's home or a new temporary directory. The session writes the script to a file called `inventory`. The first line chooses Bash. `"$@"` expands to one argument per input, preserving the original boundaries.

Check the script syntax before running it.

`bash` runs a shell script. With -n it checks syntax without executing the script.

Set owner execute permission with `chmod u+x inventory`.

Use `printf 'abc' > 'day one'`.

The absence of a trailing newline makes the expected size three bytes. Run `./inventory 'day one' missing >good 2>problems` and immediately save `rc=$?`.

Read the two files, then print the saved status. The valid file still appears despite the missing argument. A nonzero status carries the partial failure back to the caller.

## Change a requirement

Make a zero-length regular file and a directory whose name contains a space. Run the script with each alone, both together and no arguments. Build a table of input, output stream and exit status **before** running them. Finally modify a copy of the script to count successful regular files and print a summary, including when there are zero. Keep its exit-status contract.

**Check your work.** An empty regular file is valid with a byte count of zero. A directory produces a diagnostic and status 1. No arguments produces usage and status 2. Mixed inputs produce evidence for both cases. Swapping the argument order must preserve the overall failure. Explain why setting result back to zero on each later success would introduce a bug.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>work=$(mktemp -d)

>cd "$work"

>cat > inventory <<'ERUDIOR_FILE'
>#!/bin/bash
>if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
>    printf 'usage: inventory PATH ...\n' >&2
>    exit 2
>fi
>result=0
>for path in "$@"; do
>    if [ -f "$path" ]; then
>        bytes=$(wc -c < "$path") || exit 1
>        printf '%s bytes\t%s\n' "$bytes" "$path"
>    else
>        printf 'not a regular file: %s\n' "$path" >&2
>        result=1
>    fi
>done
>exit "$result"
>ERUDIOR_FILE

>bash -n inventory

>chmod u+x inventory

>printf 'abc' > 'day one'

>./inventory 'day one' missing >good 2>problems

>rc=$?

>cat good
3 bytes	day one
>cat problems
not a regular file: missing
>echo "$rc"
1
```

lessons.title: Lab • Deliver an executable classifier
lessons.body:
On the **client**, install `/usr/local/bin/lab-classify` as an executable shell script for an unprivileged user. Given one nonnegative integer, it must print exactly `small` below 10 and `large` for 10 or higher. The command should run directly by absolute path.

Write your own tests first. Include 0, 9, 10 and a larger value you choose. Run them as `learner` and compare the exact standard output. If a root-run test works and a learner test fails, inspect the shebang, directory traversal and file mode. Extra prompts or debug output on stdout change the result.

## Reason through a reported result

Running sh /usr/local/bin/lab-classify 10 prints large; executing the file by its full path as learner returns Permission denied. Which part of the contract failed?

**Check your reasoning.** Calling sh reads the script as input and bypasses the direct-execution check. Inspect execute permission and ancestor traversal, then test the full path as learner.

lessons.title: Trace a file down to the disk that holds it
lessons.body:
A directory is a location in the names you can walk through. A filesystem is the structure that stores names, data and metadata. A mount attaches the root of a filesystem at a directory. A partition is a bounded region of a disk. LVM adds another layer that lets logical volumes draw from a shared pool of storage. The size of a disk, a logical volume and a mounted filesystem can legitimately differ.

## Work backwards from a file

Use the terminal session on your VM.

Read SOURCE, TARGET and FSTYPE. Use `lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS` to follow the mount's source toward a disk.

On a machine using LVM it may go through a logical volume and a partition. On a simpler installation the filesystem can occupy a partition directly. Compare `df -hT /` with `du -sh ~/shift-practice` if that directory exists.

`df` reports filesystem capacity and free space. The -T option includes filesystem type.

`du` totals the space used by files and directories. Use -s for a single total and -h for readable units.

The first reports capacity of the containing filesystem. The second totals a particular directory tree.

**Read this case.** A guest has a 20 GiB virtual disk. One partition occupies 12 GiB and its volume group has 4 GiB free. A mounted XFS logical volume of 5 GiB is full. If you need 1 GiB more there, allocating a new virtual disk is unnecessary. Check free extents in `vgs`, enlarge the correct logical volume, grow the filesystem, then verify the mount gained capacity.

`vgs` lists LVM volume groups, their size and their unassigned capacity.

Equality between `lsblk` disk size and `df` space would be the wrong success criterion.

## Identify a new practice disk

On a manual VM record your current `lsblk` tree.

Power it off, attach one new, empty 2 GiB virtual disk and boot it. Identify the added device by the before/after inventory, size, mountpoints, children and any filesystem signatures. Run `sudo wipefs --no-act DEVICE` with the newly identified path to inspect signatures without changing it. If you cannot distinguish the data disk from the boot disk, use the new temporary file and loop procedure in the next lesson.

**Independent ticket.** Draw the actual layers serving / on your machine. Circle the layer where unused space would need to exist before you could extend an existing LV. Keep a copy of this inventory for comparison after your storage workshop.

```plaintext
>lsblk -o NAME,TYPE,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS

>vgs
```

lessons.title: Draw a partition table before changing a disk
lessons.body:
A disk is a sequence of addressable blocks. GPT is a table that describes which ranges belong to partitions. An empty partition still needs a consumer, such as a filesystem, swap or an LVM physical volume. A mountpoint is a directory in the running system. Knowing a directory's name does not identify which disk you are about to change.

## Provision a miniature disk inside the client

Use the ordinary learner account in the disposable practice guest. This exercise uses a newly created file as a disk, so your system disk and the course's extra disks can stay attached. Install `parted` from the trusted DVD if it is absent. Have 160 MiB of space available. Keep the same terminal open so the variables remain available.

`truncate` sets a file's logical size. An enlarged image can be sparse until data is written.

`losetup` associates an image file with a loop device. The --find and --show options select an available device and print its name.

Stop until the reported backing path is exactly your new `training.img` and there are no mounts on that loop device. The next command writes a new partition table. Use only this verified loop device. A MiB is 1,048,576 bytes. Starting at 1 MiB leaves space for the table and aligns the partition.

`parted` reads or edits a disk partition table. Its first device argument determines which disk will change.

`partprobe` asks the kernel to reread the partition table for a changed device.

`udevadm` interacts with the device manager. The settle operation waits for queued device events.

The first partition is about 64 MiB. It has no filesystem yet. Free space remains after it. Predict where a second 48 MiB partition could fit without changing the start or end of the first. Create it using `sudo parted -s "$loop" mkpart later 65MiB 113MiB`.

Reread the table and check both ranges. A GPT partition name identifies a table entry; a filesystem label is written by a filesystem tool inside that entry.

## Reverse one change

Remove only the second partition on this new loop disk. Prove the first partition's number, start and end are unchanged and the old second range is free again. Then detach the loop device. The backing file keeps the partition table. Reattaching with `--partscan` lets you inspect it again.

**Check your work.** On this two-partition practice table, `sudo parted -s "$loop" rm 2` removes entry 2.

After `partprobe`, `udevadm settle` and `print free`, entry 1 still spans 1–65 MiB.

Use `sudo losetup -d "$loop"` after verifying that neither partition is mounted.

In the following LVM workshop you will build a different, larger disk and follow its layers all the way to a file.

lessons.title: Build and extend a disposable LVM volume
lessons.body:
A department needs a filesystem that can grow without moving its existing data. A partition can hold an LVM physical volume (PV). A volume group (VG) pools capacity. A logical volume (LV) draws space from the pool. Growing the LV and growing the filesystem are distinct operations.

## Self-check using a new file as a practice disk

Use a disposable AlmaLinux 10 guest with loop devices, parted, LVM2 and XFS tools. Use the same root shell for the whole session (`sudo -i`).

Use only the newly allocated loop device reported below. Stop if `vgs workshp_vg` already finds a group with that name, or `/mnt/workshp_lv` is already in use.

This exercise needs about 1 GiB of free space. The regular-file disk lets you practice without repartitioning a system disk.

Confirm the partition path shown by `lsblk` equals `$part`.

If the LVM devices file is in use and the partition is not visible to LVM, add only the practice partition with `lvmdevices --adddev "$part"`.

`lvmdevices` manages which devices LVM is allowed to use on systems with a devices file.

An image filtering loop devices may require an attached unused training disk instead. Do not substitute the boot disk.

`pvcreate` initializes a verified, unused exercise partition as an LVM physical volume.

`vgcreate` combines named physical volumes into a new volume group.

`lvcreate` allocates a logical volume from free space in a volume group.

`mkfs.xfs` creates a new XFS filesystem on the chosen device and replaces any previous filesystem there.

`mount` attaches a filesystem to a directory so lookups under that path enter the mounted filesystem.

`lvextend` adds capacity to an existing logical volume. A plus before the size requests an increase and -r also requests filesystem growth.

`lvs` lists logical volumes and their sizes.

Expect more space and unchanged proof text. `-r` requests a matching filesystem resize. Use `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs` to find which layer lacks space if growth fails.

`pvs` lists physical volumes and their volume group membership.

A loop mapping lasts only for this exercise. Practice mounting by UUID across reboot on an attached practice disk in the next module.

## Clean up the disk you created

After confirming `losetup "$loop"` still shows your temporary file and `findmnt /mnt/workshp_lv` identifies your practice LV, unmount it.

Remove the practice LV, then the VG, then its PV label using `lvremove /dev/workshp_vg/reports`, `vgremove workshp_vg` and `pvremove "$part"`.

`lvremove` removes the named logical volume and its data.

`vgremove` removes an empty volume group from LVM.

`pvremove` removes the LVM physical-volume label from the specified exercise device.

If you added the partition to the LVM devices file, remove its entry if still present. Delete partition 1 on that loop disk with `parted -s "$loop" rm 1`, detach with `losetup -d "$loop"`, then remove your temporary file and empty mount directory.

Check `lvs` and `losetup -j "$diskfile"` to confirm retirement.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>sudo -i

>vgs workshp_vg
  Volume group "workshp_vg" not found
  Cannot process volume group workshp_vg
>diskfile=$(mktemp /var/tmp/rhcsa-disk.XXXXXX)

>truncate -s 1G "$diskfile"

>loop=$(losetup --find --show --partscan "$diskfile")

>losetup "$loop"
/dev/loop0: [64768]:19020 (/var/tmp/rhcsa-disk.K7Z3h2)
>parted -s "$loop" mklabel gpt mkpart primary 1MiB 100%

>partprobe "$loop"

>udevadm settle

>part="$loop"p1

>lsblk -o PATH,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE "$loop"
PATH            SIZE TYPE FSTYPE
/dev/loop0        1G loop
/dev/loop0p1   1022M part
>lsblk
NAME   MAJ:MIN RM  SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS
sr0     11:0    1   68K  0 rom
vda    252:0    0   10G  0 disk
|-vda1 252:1    0    1M  0 part
|-vda2 252:2    0  200M  0 part /boot/efi
|-vda3 252:3    0    1G  0 part /boot
`-vda4 252:4    0  8.8G  0 part /
>lsblk -o PATH,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE "$loop"
PATH          SIZE TYPE FSTYPE
/dev/loop0      1G loop
/dev/loop0p1 1022M part
>lvmdevices --adddev "$part"

>pvcreate "$part"
  Physical volume "/dev/loop0p1" successfully created.
>vgcreate workshp_vg "$part"
  Volume group "workshp_vg" successfully created
>lvcreate -L 400M -n reports workshp_vg
```

lessons.title: Activate swap and make it return at startup
lessons.body:
Swap supplies extra backing space for idle memory pages. An allocated file, a swap signature, activation now and a boot-time entry are four distinct states. On the untimed server inspect `free -h`, `swapon --show --bytes`, `df -h /var/lib` and `findmnt -T /var/lib`.

`swapon` reports active swap with --show and activates swap when given a prepared swap file or device.

Use the following on the workshop guest's local XFS or ext4 filesystem. Choose a fresh path and ensure at least 70 MiB is free.

`sh` runs a shell. Its -c option executes the quoted command string as one script. `dd` copies bytes. Here a block size and count specify the exact length written from /dev/zero.

If creation failed or the path already existed, stop and choose a new path. Inspect the resulting regular file and mode with `sudo stat /var/lib/workshop.swap`.

Initialize your new file with `sudo mkswap /var/lib/workshop.swap` and activate it with `sudo swapon /var/lib/workshop.swap`.

`mkswap` writes a swap signature to the specified exercise file or device.

Verify the name and size with `swapon --show --bytes`.

Allocating real blocks avoids sparse-file activation errors.

Edit `/etc/fstab` and add one line `/var/lib/workshop.swap none swap defaults 0 0` after confirming that path has no existing entry. Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo findmnt --verify`.

Reboot the untimed guest and use the terminal session again.

A clean configuration file alone cannot prove that the kernel activated the space.

## Swap on a new partition or logical volume

Tasks often ask for swap on new block storage instead of a file. On a disposable guest with an attached practice disk, create a partition with `parted` (type it `linux-swap` with `mkpart swap linux-swap 1MiB 513MiB`) or a new LV with `lvcreate -L 512M -n swap2 VG`. Leave existing partitions and volumes untouched. Run `mkswap` on the new device and note the UUID it prints. Add a line such as `UUID=actual-uuid none swap defaults 0 0`, then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo swapon -a`.

Confirm the new device in `swapon --show` before and after a reboot.

A swap device has no mountpoint, so its fstab line uses `none` and the type `swap`.

lessons.title: Add capacity without disturbing existing data
lessons.body:
A branch can attach a second disk but cannot take the archive offline. A volume group can combine physical volumes so an existing logical volume can grow. The existing filesystem keeps its identity. Your job is to prove both that the data survived and that the new capacity reached the application.

On a disposable manual VM, attach two fresh virtual disks of 2 GiB each. Take an inventory before and after, then work only on these confirmed empty disks. Use the GPT and LVM workshop procedure on the first disk to make a VG named branchtest and a 512 MiB LV called inbox. Give it ext4 with `mkfs.ext4`, mount it at /mnt/branchtest and create a file containing a handoff note. Record its checksum and `df -B1 /mnt/branchtest`.

Leave existing system partitions and VGs alone.

Use `sudo parted DEVICE print` to identify the second disposable disk, replacing DEVICE with its verified path. A blank disk can report an unrecognized disk label. Following the partitioning procedure in the LVM workshop, create a GPT with one partition, settle device discovery and inspect the new partition path. In the commands below set `newpart` to that actual partition. On a host using the LVM devices file, add that practice partition to the devices file if necessary.

`vgextend` adds another physical volume to an existing volume group.

`resize2fs` resizes an ext2, ext3 or ext4 filesystem. Without a size it grows to the available block-device capacity.

The LV grows first. resize2fs expands the mounted ext4 filesystem to use the larger device. An XFS filesystem instead grows online through its mountpoint with xfs_growfs. The earlier workshop used lvextend -r to request both operations together. Read the note again and compare its checksum. A larger LV with an unchanged filesystem size is unfinished work.

**Independent ticket.** Report the new PV, the VG's remaining free space, the larger filesystem and the matching checksum. Use the mount-by-UUID exercise to add persistence on your clone. For cleanup, remove any practice fstab entry, reload systemd, unmount your test filesystem, and retire the LV, VG and both PV labels only after identifying each against your recorded inventory. Remove your test disks in the hypervisor only when the clone no longer depends on them.

lessons.title: Explain why a file disappears under a mount
lessons.body:
A colleague remembers putting handoff.txt in /mnt/dispatch. You see an empty directory at that location. Before deciding anyone deleted data, ask which filesystem currently supplies the path. A mount can cover files in an existing directory. Unmounting exposes them again.

On a disposable guest pick a fresh directory under your home with `work=$(mktemp -d "$HOME/mount-practice.XXXXXX")`.

Save the original marker with `printf 'underneath\n' > "$work/handoff.txt"`.

Record `findmnt -T "$work"`.

Mount a small temporary memory filesystem with `sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=8m tmpfs "$work"` and inspect `findmnt -T "$work"` and `ls -la "$work"` again.

The first marker seems to have vanished. Add a different marker with `echo visible | sudo tee "$work/live.txt"`.

Before unmounting, predict which marker will remain.

From outside the mounted directory, run `sudo umount "$work"`, then `ls -la "$work"` and `cat "$work/handoff.txt"`.

`umount` detaches the named mount so the underlying directory is visible again.

This new listing comes from the original filesystem. The temporary filesystem is gone. Remove your original marker and the empty temporary directory when finished. If a real unmount says busy, first check whether a shell is using the mount as its working directory.

**Independent ticket.** A backup job wrote 200 MiB into a directory before the data disk mounted. After the mount, the files disappear and space on the root filesystem stays low. Draw the two storage locations. State which source you would verify before moving any data. In the next workshop, use a marker, a UUID and a reboot to prove which filesystem serves a path.

lessons.title: Prove which filesystem contains a user's report
lessons.body:
A newly mounted empty filesystem can make an existing directory appear empty. The files previously visible there still belong to the filesystem underneath it. If an operator writes a new report before the intended filesystem is mounted, it may disappear from view after the mount returns. Use a small temporary filesystem to see both sides of this problem.

## Observe one pathname backed by two sources

On the untimed client, create a new directory. Capture its current source and filesystem type before mounting anything on it.

The name `before` is now hidden. The mount changed what path resolution reaches when it enters `reports`. `tmpfs` stores its files in memory-backed storage. It is a useful stand-in for a second filesystem because the mount starts empty. Create evidence **inside** the mount with `printf 'temporary view\n' | sudo tee "$work/reports/during"`.

Record the source for that file and check the original marker is absent.

## Reverse it and explain the ticket

Unmount the temporary filesystem from outside the mount.

List the directory again and read the original marker.

Predict which file will be visible. This tmpfs loses its contents when its last mount is removed. A disk-backed filesystem would retain its data on that disk.

**Check your work.** `before` is back and `during` is gone from the pathname. Write a brief response to a user who copied a file during an NFS outage and can no longer see it once NFS returns. Explain how you would inspect each backing filesystem on a practice system without deleting or overwriting either copy. For a real persistent mount, add the device UUID, expected type and a post-reboot file check to your handoff.

lessons.title: Mount the right filesystem and prove what is serving a path
lessons.body:
On the server inspect `lsblk -f`, `findmnt -T /` and `sudo blkid`.

`blkid` reads device signatures such as the filesystem type, label and UUID.

Device names can change after hardware changes. A filesystem UUID or unique label identifies the intended filesystem across boots. A mounted filesystem also hides whatever was in the mount directory underneath it.

## Self-check with disposable filesystems

Use the new-file and loop procedure in **Build and extend a disposable LVM volume** on a disposable guest, with a fresh backing file for each filesystem. For each new empty partition, choose **one** formatter: `mkfs.ext4 -L TRAINEXT "$part"`, `mkfs.xfs -L TRAINXFS "$part"`, or `mkfs.vfat -n TRAINVF "$part"`. VFAT needs dosfstools. Never reformat a partition whose data you intend to keep. Create an empty practice mountpoint, mount the partition, write and read a marker, and use `findmnt -T /path/to/marker` to record the source and type. Unmount, verify the marker disappears, remount and verify it returns. VFAT generally expresses ownership and masks through mount options.

For a boot test, use a persistent, attached practice disk. Mount its filesystem by UUID or by LABEL at a new path. For example, with an ext4 volume add a single `UUID=actual-uuid /mnt/reports ext4 defaults 0 2` line to `/etc/fstab`, using the real identifier from `blkid`. Create the mountpoint, unmount any manual mount, reload systemd, run `sudo findmnt --verify` and `sudo mount /mnt/reports`.

Verify the source and marker after a reboot. Remove the entry before retiring the disk.

## Self-check the network path

In the untimed client, mount the supplied server export once at a separate empty location. Run `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-check`, `sudo mount -t nfs -o ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects /mnt/nfs-check` and inspect the marker with `findmnt -T /mnt/nfs-check/erudior-lab.txt`.

Unmount this test with `sudo umount /mnt/nfs-check`.

Compare that manual mount with the direct map in the following NFS workshop. Autofs installs a trigger; reading a path makes the NFS mount appear. A local directory with a copied file cannot supply the live server's data.

lessons.title: Build a manual NFS client before automating access
lessons.body:
Network File System (NFS) lets a client access data another machine exports. There are two names for every shared file in this exercise. The server stores it under /srv/projects. The client will see the same bytes through a mount at a different path. Creating a local directory with a similar name cannot make it follow server changes.

On the prepared server use the terminal session and read the allowed client and access options.

`exportfs` manages the server's NFS export table. With -v it lists exports and their effective options.

On the client create an empty directory, for example `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-observe`.

Mount the share with `sudo mount -t nfs -o ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects /mnt/nfs-observe`.

Use the terminal session and read the marker.

Confirm that the source includes the server and export and the type is nfs or nfs4. Change out of the mounted path before running `sudo umount /mnt/nfs-observe`.

## Replace eager mounting with a trigger

A direct autofs map maps an absolute client pathname to a server export. The master file points to the map, autofs watches the trigger, and opening a file inside that path causes the actual NFS mount. In **Workshop: trigger a network mount from the client**, configure the two short map files. Before touching the path, examine `findmnt -t autofs`.

After reading the marker, examine `findmnt -t nfs,nfs4`.

The two listings show different stages of the request. The NFS mount can expire after inactivity while autofs keeps waiting.

**Independent ticket.** A client has the correct marker text but the source is its local root filesystem. Explain how someone could get a misleading success. On the server add a fresh marker to the same export. Read it under the client path and identify the network mount that supplied it. If manual mounting fails, investigate the export and connectivity first. If only on-demand access fails, investigate the map key, file suffix and the autofs journal.

lessons.title: Workshop: trigger a network mount from the client
lessons.body:
This dedicated two-machine workshop gives you a separate attempt to configure an on-demand NFS mount. Use **Start lab** in this lesson and log in to each console in turn. First check the server export and a manual client mount as you practiced in the preceding reading. **Check my work** verifies the on-demand mount in this workshop. Use the shared practice terminal in ordinary readings for your other experiments.

lessons.title: Read the running kernel and the next boot entry
lessons.body:
A kernel update can be installed while the machine continues running the previous kernel. There are three separate questions: which kernel packages are on disk, which kernel booted this guest, and which entry is selected by default for a future boot. Conflating them turns a routine update into a confusing incident report.

## Follow the boot chain

Firmware selects a boot device. The bootloader selects an entry containing a kernel, an initial RAM filesystem and arguments. The kernel and early userspace make the real root filesystem available. The system manager starts the selected target and its dependencies. A missing root device, an invalid optional mount, and a failing application service occur at different points in that sequence.

On the running untimed client, compare the commands below. `grubby` and the boot files live inside the guest. Use the guest console for the subsequent boot labs.

`uname` prints kernel information. Use -r for the running release or -m for the machine architecture.

`grubby` inspects and updates boot entries. A default entry describes a future boot choice.

Find the version in the default kernel path. Compare it with `uname -r` and the RPM list.

All three can agree on a newly installed guest. If multiple kernels exist, the current version and next default can differ. `/proc/cmdline` reports what this boot actually received. The systemd default target tells you which collection of units the manager should start in its normal configuration. It does not select a kernel.

## Make a boot handoff

An operator claims the latest installed kernel is already running because the package manager listed it. Collect a short handoff answering all three questions. Then record one argument from the current command line and look for it in the selected boot entry. A one-time menu edit may explain a difference. In the following boot-target lesson, test a temporary argument and confirm the normal selection returns on the next startup.

**Check your work.** Your handoff gives a running release, the installed package version or versions and an explicit default boot path. If they match, report that observation. If they differ, identify the next evidence you need before changing any default. Keep an existing working entry available during boot practice.

lessons.title: Repair a failed mount from the guest console
lessons.body:
At power-on the firmware starts the bootloader, which loads a kernel and an initial RAM filesystem. That early environment finds the real root filesystem. The kernel starts systemd, which brings up the configured target and its units. A misspelled data-volume UUID is a useful diagnostic case: the kernel may boot normally while a later mount fails.

## Rehearse recovery on a disposable clone

Use a powered-off snapshot of a VM you administer, with a working hypervisor console and a known root password for rescue login. If the root account is locked on your own clone, an authorized sudo administrator can set a temporary root password there with `sudo passwd root` before the drill.

Keep this clone separate from the timed guests. Save a known-good copy with `sudo cp -p /etc/fstab /root/fstab.before-drill`.

Run `systemctl get-default` and `findmnt -T /` and record both.

Create /mnt/drill on the clone and add the following line to /etc/fstab in an editor. The label intentionally names a nonexistent practice filesystem. The noauto flag keeps it out of the normal startup transaction.

In the editor, append `LABEL=ABSENTDRILL /mnt/drill ext4 noauto 0 0` once and save.

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and request the mount explicitly with `sudo mount /mnt/drill`.

Read the diagnostic and compare the label with `lsblk -f`.

The declared identity cannot be resolved. At the guest console reboot and use the preceding lesson's one-boot rescue target. Authenticate, compare the active target and the saved default, and fix only the added line with your editor. You can check your work against /root/fstab.before-drill using diff. Run `systemctl daemon-reload` and `findmnt --verify`.

Return to normal service, reboot, and verify the recorded default and root mount. A preexisting warning needs separate interpretation; your practice error should be gone.

**Independent ticket.** Explain at which boot stage your practice definition would matter if it were required automatically. Show how you would distinguish a missing device from a wrong filesystem type, using its signature and an observed error. The exercise leaves ordinary boot available even if you need more time to finish.

lessons.title: Recover root access by interrupting the boot
lessons.body:
A server's root password has been lost and no account with sudo remains. With console access you can stop the boot early, set a new password and let SELinux repair the changed file's label. Practice only on a disposable RHEL 10 guest whose boot menu you can reach and whose disk is not encrypted. Keep the graded pair's boot options intact.

## Reset the password from an early shell
At the GRUB menu highlight the current kernel and press `e`. On the line that starts with `linux`, remove `rhgb quiet` so messages stay visible, then append `rd.break`. Boot with the on-screen key (usually Ctrl+x). At the `switch_root` prompt the installed system is mounted read-only at `/sysroot`.

The first `exit` leaves the chroot and the second resumes startup. The relabel runs once and reboots the guest; let it finish. Log in as root with the new password and confirm with `id` and `getenforce`.

## Why the relabel matters
`passwd` writes a new `/etc/shadow`. The early shell does not load the SELinux policy, so the new file can get the wrong label, and a system with a mislabeled shadow file can reject every login. `/.autorelabel` asks the next normal boot to restore default contexts across the filesystem.

## An alternative entry point
If the early shell lacks `chroot`, edit the `linux` line again: change `ro` to `rw`, remove `rhgb quiet` and append `init=/bin/bash`. The root filesystem is then already writable at `/`. Run `passwd root` and `touch /.autorelabel`, then `exec /sbin/init` to continue startup. The two sessions are alternatives. Either way the edit applies to this boot only. Confirm afterwards with `cat /proc/cmdline` that neither argument remains.

A GRUB password, Secure Boot policy or an encrypted root volume adds its own prompt before you reach a shell. On the exam, read the task for the machine and the account it names.

## Terminal session

Use only the entry method you selected in GRUB. The rd.break session starts at the remount and ends at the second exit. The fallback session starts at the second password change and ends at exec. Run the final identity, enforcing-mode and boot-argument checks after a normal login. Read the instructions above before choosing steps.

```plaintext
>mount -o remount,rw /sysroot

>chroot /sysroot

>passwd root
New password:
Retype new password:
passwd: all authentication tokens updated successfully.
>touch /.autorelabel

>exit
exit
>exit
exit
>passwd root
New password:
Retype new password:
passwd: all authentication tokens updated successfully.
>touch /.autorelabel

>exec /sbin/init

>id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
>getenforce
Enforcing

BOOT_IMAGE=(hd0,gpt3)/vmlinuz-6.12.0-264.16.1.el10_3.x86_64 root=UUID=440e54fe-2ae7-4094-aeae-d23298fb14cf ro console=tty0 console=ttyS0,115200n8 no_timer_check biosdevname=0 net.ifnames=0
```

lessons.body:
Use the untimed pair as an approved client and server. On the server inspect `systemctl status sshd` and `ss -lnt`.

If OpenSSH server is installed but inactive, enable it with `sudo systemctl enable --now sshd`.

Use your own guest account for this exercise.

On the client use the terminal session and check that workshop_id and workshop_id.pub are unused.

Generate a dedicated key with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/workshop_id` and supply a passphrase.

`ssh-keygen` creates or inspects SSH keys. The -l and -f options together report a fingerprint for a specified key file.

Compare the server's console output from `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` with the ED25519 host fingerprint when accepting the first connection.

If the guest policy requires a different algorithm, use a supported key such as RSA with at least 3072 bits and check the host fingerprint for the algorithm actually negotiated. If SSH password login for learner is allowed, copy the public key with `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id.pub learner@192.168.77.10`.

`ssh-copy-id` installs a public key for a remote login account after authenticating to that account.

Otherwise log in locally on the server as learner, create `~/.ssh` with mode 700 and append the single line from the client's **.pub** file to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Set that file to 600 and restore its default SELinux context with `restorecon -RFv ~/.ssh`.

Only the public key is copied.

`ssh` connects to a remote host. A trailing command runs on that host and its output returns to this terminal.

The server must accept the key for this test to succeed. Your private key may still ask for its local passphrase. Then transfer your own note using `scp -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey notes.txt learner@192.168.77.10:notes.received`.

`scp` copies a file over SSH. A host followed by a colon introduces a remote path.

Create `notes.txt` locally first. Compare `sha256sum` on the two files. For a failed login, check the account, file ownership, mode, and `sudo journalctl -b -u sshd` on the server.

`firewall-cmd` inspects or configures firewalld. Select the zone serving the exercise interface before querying or changing it.

For an unused demonstration TCP port, query `sudo firewall-cmd --zone=ZONE --query-port=18080/tcp` in runtime and with `--permanent`. If neither allows it, add it first at runtime with `--add-port=18080/tcp` and repeat both queries. Make it persistent with the same add command plus `--permanent`. Reload and verify both queries. Remove only your two practice rules when finished. Opening a firewall port permits traffic to reach a listener; verify listening separately with `ss -lnt`.

`sftp` offers an interactive session over the same connection, and `rsync -av -e ssh SOURCE learner@192.168.77.10:DEST` copies only what changed when rsync is installed on both ends.

lessons.title: Test a listener and its firewall rule separately
lessons.body:
A server can allow traffic to a port where nothing is listening. It can also have a perfectly healthy listener that is unreachable from the client. To distinguish those conditions, make a request from each side of the firewall and inspect the interface's active zone.

## Set up a temporary known service

Use the untimed **server**. Identify the interface carrying `192.168.77.10` with `ip -brief address` and find its zone with `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`.

Record that exact zone as `zone=NAME` in your shell. Verify that TCP port 18082 is unused with `ss -ltn` and that neither runtime nor permanent policy has a specific rule for it.

If an existing service or rule already uses it, choose another unused practice port throughout. In an isolated course pair, run:

`python3` runs Python. With a filename it runs that script, and with -m it runs an installed Python module.

`curl` makes a request to a URL. Use -i to include response headers or -f to give a failure status for HTTP errors.

Expect the server request to return the roster. From the **client** issue the following command.

Record the baseline. If traffic is already allowed by the zone's target or a broader rule, document it. A successful baseline cannot establish that your new rule opened a blocked path.

## Demonstrate runtime and persistent policy

On the server, use the terminal session and repeat the client request.

Query both `sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$zone" --query-port=18082/tcp` and the same command with `--permanent`.

Add the permanent rule only after checking the zone and result. Reload, query both stores again and repeat the remote request. Read the server log to identify which guest actually made the request.

## Isolate one failure

Stop your temporary server process with `kill "$web"`, keeping the firewall rule in place briefly.

Try again from the client and inspect `ss` on the server. What single observation distinguishes a missing listener from the earlier firewall experiment?

**Check your work.** Report zone, listener and client response separately. Restore your baseline by removing only the practice port from each store to which you added it. Retest both queries. A firewall rule may survive boot while the short-lived Python process ends when its session ends.

## Terminal session

Keep the server shell that started Python open. Use the client for the timed connection attempts, including the retry after stopping the listener. Run socket and firewall checks in the server shell. Remove only the rule created for this exercise.

lessons.title: Bring up a small web service and locate a failed request
lessons.body:
A branch office needs an internal status page. A successful request depends on several independent conditions. The web process must start, listen on the intended address, pass filesystem and SELinux checks, and receive traffic through the correct firewall zone. Test locally first, then from the client. Use your own disposable pair with a trusted RPM source.

## Get a known-good local result

On the server install httpd and curl if needed using DNF. On a fresh server create one file with `printf 'branch ready\n' | sudo tee /var/www/html/shift-status.txt`.

Restore its normal policy label with `sudo restorecon -v /var/www/html/shift-status.txt`.

Run `sudo systemctl enable --now httpd` and `curl -i http://127.0.0.1/shift-status.txt`.

Expect an HTTP 200 status and the marker. If startup fails, inspect `sudo apachectl configtest` and `sudo journalctl -b -u httpd`.

`apachectl` controls Apache. Its configtest operation asks the server to parse its configuration.

A successful request for a different page does not establish access to this file.

With firewalld active, list `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`.

Use the dedicated private zone from **Build your own client and server**. Verify the NAT interface belongs to another zone and its rules do not already allow HTTP. For this exercise set `zone=NAME` using that actual zone. If HTTP is not already allowed, apply `sudo firewall-cmd --zone="$zone" --add-service=http`.

From the client use the terminal session.

Add the same service with `--permanent` when you intend this private service to survive a reload. Reload and repeat the client request. Record whether the rule was already present before changing anything.

**Interpret three outcomes.** A 404 means an HTTP server answered but the requested resource was not found. A 403 means HTTP answered but refused access; inspect path traversal, the server config, the journal and SELinux evidence. A timeout gives no HTTP status; check the route, address binding and firewall. In each case identify the first layer that already worked.

**Independent ticket.** Publish a second marker and request it by a lab hostname from the client. Save the status line, body and serving host. Reboot the server and repeat from the client. If you opened the rule solely for this exercise, remove only the HTTP service rule you added from both runtime and permanent configuration.

lessons.title: Diagnose access from the account that needs it
lessons.body:
An operator says a report is “permission denied” and asks for broader access to the entire server. First identify who performed the failing action, which object they attempted to access and whether they needed to read an existing file or replace it. Check ordinary permissions and directory traversal before investigating a service's SELinux domain.

## Reproduce a small failure

On the untimed client as learner, build a private directory you own. Leave the shell's working directory outside it so that the following test reflects path traversal by a new process.

The owner can read and write directory entries as permissions allow, but cannot traverse this directory without its execute bit. `cat` should fail for the ordinary account although the file's own mode allows reading. Repair just the missing permission with `chmod u+x "$work/reports"` and retry as the same learner.

Collect `stat -c '%A %U:%G %n'` on both objects. A test performed solely as root would give misleading evidence about ordinary access.

## Apply the reasoning to a service

On the server, compare `ls -Zd /var/www/html`, `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt` and `ps -eZ | grep httpd`.

A process domain is the SELinux type of a running process. A file type labels the object. A service may be denied after the ordinary identity checks succeed. If httpd is stopped, there is no running httpd worker to inspect. In the following service lab, repeat this observation with the daemon running and test the actual URL.

## Write a repair note

Given a world-readable page under a private parent directory, predict the first ordinary failure for a service account. Given a correctly traversable document root containing a file moved from a home directory, name a label comparison that could explain a second failure. Decide which layer each repair addresses.

**Check your work.** Put the failing actor, operation, path, first failing observation, smallest correction and repeated test in your note. Keep the service under enforcing policy for the later web checks. A successful `cat` as learner is evidence for that account, while an HTTP response from the client demonstrates the service path.

## Terminal session

Run the file-permission exercise on the client. Switch to the server for the web-content labels and httpd process check.

lessons.title: Diagnose a denial while keeping access controls intact
lessons.body:
A web document is readable by ordinary file mode, yet a confined service cannot access it. Check identity, traversal and standard permissions, then examine SELinux. Use `getenforce`, `ls -Zd /var/www/html`, `ps -eZ` and `sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent` when the audit tools are present.

`ausearch` searches audit events. The AVC type covers SELinux access decisions.

Compare an affected file's type with `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt`.

The policy convention for read-only web content under the normal document root is `httpd_sys_content_t`.

In the untimed server, use `sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html` if needed.

If the example.txt name is unused, create it with `sudo touch /var/www/html/example.txt`.

Compare `ls -Z /var/www/html/example.txt` with `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt`.

On this disposable file, use the terminal session.

`chcon` changes a file's current security context. The --reference option copies the context of another path.

Observe the changed type, then use the terminal session on the file you created.

A file moved from another directory can retain its old label. A copy or rename is no substitute for checking the resulting context.

## Move the policy with the application

For an alternate document root on a guest with semanage, create `/srv/workshop-web` and a test file. Add the path rule `sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/workshop-web(/.*)?'`, then apply it with `sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/workshop-web`.

`semanage` manages persistent local SELinux policy settings such as path mappings and port types.

Check actual and expected labels. For a web service that needs a different listening port, inspect `semanage port -l` and, on an unused training port with no existing specific assignment, practice `sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 18081`.

Verify the mapping and remove your new mapping with `sudo semanage port -d -p tcp 18081` when finished.

To retire the alternate document-root rule, use `sudo semanage fcontext -d '/srv/workshop-web(/.*)?'` and `sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/workshop-web`.

Firewall policy and SELinux port labels are independent.

Inspect `getsebool httpd_can_network_connect` and `semanage boolean -l`.

`getsebool` reads the current value of an SELinux boolean.

On the disposable guest, record the current boolean before the exercise. Keep this shell open while you apply and then restore the setting.

Continue after confirming the saved value. The -P option persists the selected value across boots.

To observe enforcement modes on the untimed disposable guest only, record the current mode, compare `getenforce` after `sudo setenforce 0` and `sudo setenforce 1`, and finish in enforcing mode.

`setenforce` changes runtime SELinux enforcement mode. Use getenforce to observe that state.

On this already labeled guest, check that /etc/selinux/config sets SELINUX=enforcing. Reboot and confirm `getenforce` reports Enforcing. setenforce by itself changes the running kernel.

A denial identifies a policy decision to investigate. For ordinary default permissions, compare newly created files and directories under `umask 027` in a subshell.

Expect 640 and 750 from ordinary creation modes.

**Read a denial.** In a web AVC, find scontext (the process), tcontext (the object), tclass (what kind of object) and the requested permission in braces. For a read of a file with an unexpected type, compare the expected label with matchpathcon before changing policy. If a repair alters a label in place but restorecon reverses it, persist the intended path mapping with semanage fcontext and apply it. Confirm by serving the actual page under enforcement.

`umask` changes only the current shell.

To keep a value for one user's future shells, add a line such as `umask 027` to that user's `~/.bashrc`. For all users' login shells, put it in a new script under `/etc/profile.d/` with a `.sh` name. Open a new login and use the terminal session to verify.

lessons.title: Lab • Repair a web document label
lessons.body:
On the **server**, create the regular file `/var/www/html/erudior-status.txt` and give it the SELinux type for ordinary read-only web content, `httpd_sys_content_t`. Leave enforcement enabled. A short status line of your choice is sufficient.

Inspect the actual file type and context, the expected default context for this path, and the global enforcement mode. Avoid following a symlink to an unrelated file. If a relabel changes the type back, inspect the path's persistent policy mapping. Submit after the actual file and mode satisfy the task.

## Reason through a reported result

The document is 0644 and its expected context is httpd_sys_content_t, but ls -Z shows a home-directory type. What comparison will prove the repair?

**Check your reasoning.** Compare actual and expected types after applying the persistent label convention. Keep enforcement active and check the actual document on the next boot.

lessons.title: Lab • Serve web content on a custom port
lessons.body:
On the **server**, make `httpd` serve `/var/www/html` on TCP port 18080, running now and at boot. Allow the port through firewalld permanently and keep SELinux enforcing.

Three controls must agree. Add `Listen 18080` in `/etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf` or a file in `/etc/httpd/conf.d/`. Give that port the web-server SELinux type and allow it through the private interface’s firewall zone. Use the following on the server. If the port already has a label, inspect it before making a change.

On a manual pair, substitute the private interface’s active zone. Apply the saved rule, then start Apache.

If Apache fails to start, inspect its journal on the server.

Repeat the HTTP check from the client.

The grader checks the service, the listener, the firewall rule, enforcing mode and an HTTP answer, then repeats after a reboot.

lessons.title: Lab • Key-based SSH login between the machines
lessons.body:
Create the user `labssh` on the **server**. On the **client**, let the `learner` account log in to the server as `labssh` with an SSH key and no password prompt.

On the client as learner, create a practice key if you need one. Keep any existing key. On this disposable attempt, an empty passphrase allows the grader to log in unattended.

Install the client’s public key for labssh on the server. If the lab permits password login, run the following on the client after checking the server’s host-key fingerprint.

If the server refuses password logins, use its console to append that public line to `/home/labssh/.ssh/authorized_keys`. The directory should be mode 700 and the file 600, both owned by labssh. If you created them elsewhere, restore their SELinux contexts on the server.

On the client, first verify the server host-key fingerprint against the server console and establish trust. Then test unattended authentication as learner.

The grader runs the same kind of test as learner on the client, before and after the client reboots.
