lessons.title: Rehearsal • Hand off a working file service
lessons.body:
A shift change is approaching. The client needs an operator and a way to find and consume the server's data. The server needs a private team workspace and a dependable startup service. Use the five task cards below as the acceptance criteria. This timed rehearsal starts with fresh machines. It does not inherit work from the individual labs.

Before opening a console, draw two columns headed Client and Server. Allocate 5 minutes to map the tasks, 30 to implement them and 15 to test as the affected user. Verify the lookup and mount from the client. Verify ownership and startup behavior on the server. Partition your checks so a failure in one area does not mask evidence in another. For example, test address routing independently of hostname lookup.

Each task is worth 10 points. After submission identify the first missing observation and return to the corresponding lab. Aim to earn all 50 points before moving on.

## Reason through a reported result

The client resolves the correct address, but an NFS marker comes from the root volume. The server’s team directory passes. Which task remains open?

**Check your reasoning.** The client mount still needs a working trigger. Keep the passing server evidence separate, then verify the mount by remote source and a fresh server marker.

On a manually prepared pair, use the same task cards as the brief. For each one, record what works before and after restarting the affected guest. Use the self-check to track your own practice.

lessons.title: Rehearsal • Bring a branch server back into service
lessons.body:
A branch office is returning to service. Its client needs a usable software source and a command an ordinary operator can execute. Its server needs memory backing, a tuning policy and a document with the correct security label. Work from the five task cards below. Use a fresh evidence sheet and solve them without consulting the earlier command examples.

Reserve the last 10 minutes for verification. Record the repository ID, two classifier boundary results, the active profile, usable swap and the file context. If a persistent setting looks right on disk, identify the live query that establishes it has actually taken effect. Submit once you have tested the operator's experience. Each task is worth 10 points.

Review both columns of the result. If everything passed before reboot but one item failed afterward, name the component responsible for restoring that item at boot. Repeat the corresponding focused lab before the final practical.

## Reason through a reported result

Both the tuning profile and the web label are correct after restart. A script passes for 9 but prints small for 10. Which change has the narrowest scope?

**Check your reasoning.** Repair the script boundary and rerun it as an ordinary client user. Keep the independently verified server states intact.

On a manually prepared pair, use the same task cards as the brief. For each one, record what works before and after restarting the affected guest. Use the self-check to track your own practice.

lessons.title: Independent practical: provision a branch archive
lessons.body:
A research branch is opening. Its manager requests a durable archive, a 06:15 receipt and a private status page. You receive a fresh disposable AlmaLinux 10 server, a client, a trusted RPM source and one new 2 GiB virtual disk on the server. Use your own pair or clones set aside for this exercise. The Erudior timed form uses separate machines. Budget 75 minutes for delivery and 30 for acceptance and repair. Use installed documentation. Keep the acceptance checks below folded away in your notes until you have attempted the work.

## Work order

1. Give the server an additional client-resolvable alias, archive.branch.test, on the private network. Create a local group called archivists and a regular user called mika on the server. Give mika membership in archivists and a password maximum age of 60 days. 2. On the **new disk only**, create one GPT partition, an LVM physical volume, a volume group called branchvg and a 512 MiB logical volume called records. Create an XFS filesystem and mount it persistently by UUID at /srv/records. Keep a marker file named origin with the value branch-one. 3. Give /srv/records to group archivists with mode 2770. As mika create a note. Increase the filesystem capacity by at least 192 MiB and retain both files. Verify a fresh group login can use the archive. 4. On the server install an executable called /usr/local/bin/branch-count. For each readable filename passed as an argument print its number of lines and its original name. If no argument is supplied, exit nonzero and write a diagnostic. Make it handle a filename containing spaces. 5. Configure a systemd calendar timer to record a journal entry tagged branch-receipt every day at 06:15 server time. The corresponding service must be safe to start manually. Enable the schedule and show evidence of one actual execution. 6. Serve /branch.txt over HTTP on the private interface with the text archive online. Keep SELinux enforcing. Open only the needed firewall service in the private zone. Test from the client using the new name.

## Acceptance record

Award one practice point for each numbered row that you can demonstrate. For persistent settings, require the same outcome after a normal server reboot. A script exercise is complete when the actual inputs produce the required output and exit statuses. Record a failed row and the observed result before you consult the worked lessons.

| Row | Independent observation |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | On the client, the alias resolves to the server's private address. A fresh server login for mika shows archivists. The aging report shows 60 days. |
| 2 | The mounted source's UUID matches the boot configuration. The marker came from XFS on branchvg/records. |
| 3 | Both files survive growth and reboot. A newly created file inherits archivists and the mounted directory has mode 2770. |
| 4 | Try a zero-line file, a two-line file with a space in its name, and no arguments. Inspect stdout, stderr and status separately. |
| 5 | Query the next scheduled activation. Start the paired service and find a new tagged event. Confirm the timer is waiting after reboot. |
| 6 | From the client, request the named host and exact resource. Capture HTTP 200 and the marker together. Check enforcement on the server. Identify the private interface’s zone and check the HTTP rule there in runtime and permanent configuration. Confirm the NAT zone does not already grant HTTP access. |

**Debrief.** If the marker disappeared, compare the filesystem serving the path before and after reboot. If a file has the wrong group, inspect the mounted directory and a newly created child. If the service works locally, test its private address, then the client's lookup and the firewall. Repeat any failed row on a fresh snapshot with new names. This is a self-scored practical; the next lesson records a separate machine-graded result in the desktop app.

lessons.title: Final • RHCSA practice exam for RHEL 10
lessons.body:
You have a new client, a new server and three hours. Read the ten tasks in the exam panel. Use the named machine for each and decide your own order. Both lab machines must identify as AlmaLinux 10. Check the client and server distribution shown with the attempt. Red Hat administers the actual EX200 exam on RHEL 10.

Choose **Prepare machines**. When ready, choose **Begin**. You may use the documentation installed in the guests. For an independent rehearsal, put course notes aside until you submit. Keep a short record of which task works now and what will make it work at boot. Reserve time to test from the client's or service user's point of view.

**Submit exam** closes the consoles. The grader checks the requested state at submission, restarts the relevant machines and checks again. A task earns its 30 points when both checks pass. The ten tasks total 300 practice points, with an Erudior target of 210. Results appear in this lesson and in course **Progress**. The numerical VM result records practical performance. A lesson completion checkmark records study progress. Use **Review task checks** and the next lesson to plan a retake.

Erudior authored this fixed practice form using the published EX200 objectives. Its tasks, weights and passing target are Erudior's own. A repeat uses the same form, so use the transfer exercises in the next lesson to judge whether you can apply the skill to a new request.

## On your own pair

The ten task descriptions in the exam panel are also your manual work order. Start from the prepared snapshots in **Build your own client and server**. Set a three-hour timer. For each task record the guest, the user affected, the live result, and the result after a normal reboot. Only a desktop submission produces an Erudior VM score. If studying without a machine, predict the two observations for each task, then return for the hands-on run.

## Start another attempt

In the graded desktop exam, save the result, select **Reset exam disks**, then **Prepare machines**. For independent practice with the manual kit, use the terminal session on the host.

This discards the previous manual attempt across both guests.

lessons.title: Randomized RHCSA practice exam
lessons.body:
You have a new client, a new server and three hours. **Prepare machines** draws this attempt's ten tasks, one for each published objective area, with its own names, sizes, ports and addresses. The tasks appear when you choose **Begin**. Use the named machine for each and decide your own order. Both machines should identify as AlmaLinux 10 during preparation.

You may use the documentation installed in the guests. For an independent rehearsal, put course notes aside until you submit. Keep a short record of which task works now and what will make it work at boot. Reserve time to test from the client's or service user's point of view.

**Submit exam** closes the consoles. The grader checks the requested state at submission, restarts the relevant machines and checks again. A task earns its 30 points when both checks pass. The ten tasks total 300 practice points, with an Erudior target of 210. Results appear in this lesson and in course **Progress**. Use **Review task checks** and the next lesson to plan a retake.

A retake draws a new form. Some areas have several kinds of task (for example, local storage can be a logical volume, swap on a new device or a swap file), so a second attempt tests whether the skill transfers rather than whether you remember the last one. Erudior authored these tasks from the published EX200 objectives; the tasks, weights and passing target are Erudior's own.

lessons.title: Read your result and plan a targeted retake
lessons.body:
If you used your own machines, take the same two observations from your acceptance record. A browser study session can use the cases in the lab lessons to rehearse diagnosis. Keep the machine-verified score for work actually submitted in Erudior desktop.

Open **Progress**, then return to the final exam lesson and expand **Review task checks**. Pick one task. Record the target machine, the requested end state, what you observed at submission and what the grader observed after reboot. For any lost points, identify a specific change and one command that would expose its absence.

| Report area | Revisit this lab | Independent transfer exercise in the untimed pair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Essential tools | Hand off a team workspace | Make a second group's directory and verify the group of a newly created child. |
| Users and groups | Add a client operator | Add a second group without removing the first and test through a fresh login. |
| Software management | Bring an offline RPM source online | Give the supplied shelf a new repository ID and refresh metadata with only that ID enabled. |
| Shell scripts | Deliver an executable classifier | Use a threshold of 25 and demonstrate both boundary cases as an ordinary user. |
| Running systems | Apply a persistent performance profile | Select a different installed profile and confirm it after startup. |
| Local storage | Add persistent swap capacity | Activate a different-sized swap file and compare its requested and usable sizes. |
| File systems | Recover a share on demand | Mount the same export on demand at a different client path and prove its source. |
| Deployment and maintenance | Restore a startup service | Write your own oneshot that creates a different marker in /run on each boot. |
| Basic networking | Make the file server discoverable | Add a new alias, then distinguish an address lookup from a reachability test. |
| Security | Repair a web document label | Use a second document path and verify expected and actual types after restorecon. |

**Failed at submission:** reproduce the symptom in the affected account and guest. Check prerequisites, names, paths and active state before persistence. **Passed at submission, failed after reboot:** inspect startup enablement, persistent configuration and the new boot's journal. **Both checks passed:** attempt the transfer exercise with new names or values and explain why it still works. If grading was interrupted, reopen the lesson and use **Retry grading** where offered. A technical interruption and an observed incorrect configuration need different follow-up.

A retake uses **Reset exam disks** in the final lesson. Copy any notes or scores you want to compare first. Starting over removes that attempt's guest changes. Practice until you can verify a fresh configuration unaided, including the independent exercises outside the ten machine-graded tasks.

## Keep the official scope handy

Review the published objective list alongside your results. The RHEL manuals give the command syntax and platform conventions used throughout the course.

- [Red Hat EX200 objectives and exam format](https://www.redhat.com/en/services/training/ex200-red-hat-certified-system-administrator-rhcsa-exam)
- [Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10)
- [AlmaLinux downloads and checksums](https://almalinux.org/get-almalinux/)
- [NetworkManager nmcli examples](https://networkmanager.dev/docs/api/latest/nmcli-examples.html)
- [Flatpak remotes, installation and removal](https://docs.flatpak.org/en/latest/using-flatpak.html)

lessons.title: Optional workshop: keep data when a container is replaced
lessons.body:
This extension follows the container topics in Sander van Vugt's public training outline. Red Hat's published RHEL 10 EX200 task list is the scope for the graded course. Complete this optional workshop after your practical review. Use an untimed guest with rootless Podman configured for learner and an approved local Linux image containing `/bin/sh`. On a disconnected guest, use the offline image recipe in the reference for this lesson. No public registry is needed for that route.

## Observe three lifetimes

An image supplies a starting filesystem. A container adds an individual writable layer and runs a process. A named volume can outlive any one container. As learner use the terminal session and set `image` to the full local image name or ID.

`podman` manages container images, containers and persistent volumes in the current user's container store.

Ensure the names `rhcsa-note` and `rhcsa-ledger` are unused. Use `--pull=never` to keep the experiment on the prepared image.

The first container exited when its shell finished. Its writable layer disappeared when you removed the container. The second container prints `retained`, because it attaches the same volume. `podman volume inspect rhcsa-ledger` identifies the volume.

After inspecting it, remove only that volume.

## Explain image-based delivery

A containerized application shares the host kernel. A bootable operating-system image can instead describe the system delivered to a machine. In RHEL image mode an administrator can build and deploy a bootable image and inspect the deployed image with `bootc status` on an image-mode system.

`bootc` reports and manages image-based operating system deployments.

The course's installer-built AlmaLinux guests use conventional package management. Use a diagram or three sentences to distinguish changing a running container, rebuilding its image, and delivering a new host OS deployment.

**Check your work.** Give the two container identities or runs, the first exit status, the retained text and the reason the original `/note` disappeared. A container image tag identifies a name that can move to another image. Recording the ID or digest makes a handoff reproducible.

## Terminal session

```plaintext
>podman images
REPOSITORY                  TAG       IMAGE ID      CREATED        SIZE
localhost/rhcsa-shell       practice  823ac5bc043e  2 minutes ago  2.1 MB
>podman volume create rhcsa-ledger
rhcsa-ledger
>podman run --pull=never --name rhcsa-note -v rhcsa-ledger:/ledger "$image" /bin/sh -c 'echo temporary > /note; echo retained > /ledger/entry'

>podman ps -a --filter name=rhcsa-note
CONTAINER ID  IMAGE                           COMMAND     CREATED        STATUS                    PORTS  NAMES
9e7d45f6a110  localhost/rhcsa-shell:practice  /bin/sh -c   5 seconds ago  Exited (0) 4 seconds ago         rhcsa-note
>podman inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}' rhcsa-note
0
>podman rm rhcsa-note
rhcsa-note
>podman run --pull=never --rm -v rhcsa-ledger:/ledger "$image" /bin/sh -c 'test ! -e /note && read -r result < /ledger/entry && echo "$result"'
retained
>podman volume inspect rhcsa-ledger
[
    {
        "Name": "rhcsa-ledger",
        "Mountpoint": "/home/learner/.local/share/containers/storage/volumes/rhcsa-ledger/_data",
    }
]
>bootc status
ERROR: Not a bootc system
```

banks.title: RHEL 10 administration knowledge checks
banks.description: Predict an outcome, interpret an observation or select the next diagnostic test. Use the practicals to demonstrate the change on a machine.

questions.stem: Two consoles look identical. What most reliably tells you which guest you are about to change?
choices: Compare the shell prompt characters on both machines.
Check its hostname and interface address.
Compare the default login account names.
questions.explanation: The prompt and tools can match on both machines. The seeded server uses .10 and the client uses .20.

questions.stem: When does the timed practical start counting down?
choices: When you import the course.
When you first open a console in the untimed lab.
When you select Begin after guest preparation.
questions.explanation: Preparation and first boot precede the timer. Leaving a running timed lesson does not pause its deadline.

questions.stem: You rename a log on the same filesystem. Which name can still read the original data without any repair?
choices: A second hard link to the same inode.
A symbolic link targeting the old pathname.
A symbolic link in the parent directory targeting the old pathname.
questions.explanation: A hard link is another name for the inode. A symbolic link follows the path stored in the link.

questions.stem: New files in a project directory must inherit its group. What setting belongs on the directory?
choices: The sticky bit alone.
Setgid and appropriate group access.
Group write permission alone.
questions.explanation: Setgid controls group inheritance. The ordinary group mode controls reading, creation and traversal.

questions.stem: An existing operator needs one more group and must retain two current groups. Which command does that?
choices: usermod -G dispatch fieldops
usermod -g dispatch fieldops
usermod -aG dispatch fieldops
questions.explanation: Append preserves other supplementary memberships. A fresh login loads the updated group list.

questions.stem: Which evidence shows both the maximum password age and warning period for a local account?
choices: chage -l with the account name
getent group with the account name
passwd -S without the target account name
questions.explanation: chage -l reads the account-aging fields. A group lookup shows memberships, and passwd -S without a name reports only the calling account.

questions.stem: The file is /media/content/repodata/repomd.xml. Which local repository URL points to its root?
choices: file:///media/content/repodata/repomd.xml
file:///media/content
file:///media
questions.explanation: DNF builds the metadata path beneath baseurl. The root contains the repodata directory.

questions.stem: A learner installed a Flatpak with --user. Where should they first look for the installed app?
choices: rpm -qa
dnf repolist --enabled
flatpak list --user --app
questions.explanation: A per-user Flatpak belongs to that account’s Flatpak installation. RPM inventory and DNF source listings describe different objects.

questions.stem: A script has two filename arguments, one containing a space. How should its loop expand the positional parameters?
choices: Use a double-quoted expansion of the at-sign parameter.
Use a double-quoted expansion of the asterisk parameter.
Expand only the first positional argument.
questions.explanation: A loop using the double-quoted at-sign expansion receives one item per original argument, so the name with a space stays intact. The quoted asterisk form joins the names into one item. Reading only the first argument drops the second file.

questions.stem: A classifier changes category at 5. Which pair best detects a misplaced less-than-or-equal comparison?
choices: 0 and 1
4 and 5
12 and 13
questions.explanation: Adjacent inputs on opposite sides of the threshold reveal whether the threshold itself is in the intended category.

questions.stem: A background process moves from nice 5 to nice 10. What usually happens when CPU time is contested?
choices: It takes priority over normal processes with smaller nice values.
It is capped at ten percent of a CPU.
Other normal-priority processes get preference over it.
questions.explanation: Increasing the nice value lowers its scheduling priority. It remains eligible to run.

questions.stem: A failure happened before the last reboot. Which first query narrows the investigation to the affected boot and service?
choices: journalctl -b -1 -u NAME
journalctl -b -u NAME
systemctl list-unit-files
questions.explanation: The -1 boot offset selects the previous boot. That boot must have been retained by the journal.

questions.stem: How can you use rescue.target for one boot while keeping the configured startup default?
choices: Set rescue.target as the default indefinitely.
Select it with a one-time kernel command-line argument in GRUB.
Remove multi-user.target as a dependency from a single service.
questions.explanation: GRUB entry edits at the boot menu apply to that invocation. systemctl set-default changes normal future boots.

questions.stem: An LV grew by 128 MiB, but df shows the old XFS size. What should you check next?
choices: Whether df needs the UUID in /etc/fstab to display the new size.
Whether unmounting alone will make XFS grow to the new size.
Whether the mounted XFS filesystem was grown as well.
questions.explanation: Device capacity and filesystem capacity are tracked separately. Inspect lvs and df, then grow the mounted XFS filesystem when needed.

questions.stem: Which order follows storage from backing device to usable LVM space?
choices: Physical volume, volume group, logical volume, filesystem.
Filesystem, volume group, partition, logical volume.
Logical volume, partition, physical volume, volume group.
questions.explanation: A VG pools physical volumes. An LV allocates extents from that pool and can hold a filesystem.

questions.stem: Which observation after a reboot demonstrates that a swap file is in use by the kernel?
choices: The file exists with mode 600.
Its path appears in swapon --show.
Its path appears once in /etc/fstab.
questions.explanation: Mode and configuration support activation. swapon --show reports the active swap areas.

questions.stem: Why use the filesystem UUID in a persistent mount entry?
choices: It makes a mount succeed even when its backing disk is missing.
It makes a mount independent of its filesystem driver.
It identifies the filesystem even if the device name changes.
questions.explanation: A filesystem UUID is independent of disk discovery order. Check the identifier and filesystem type before rebooting.

questions.stem: The autofs service is active. What is the best next test of the end-user outcome?
choices: Open the remote marker through its client path, then inspect the mounted source and type.
List the local mountpoint without opening its contents.
Count entries in /etc/exports on the client.
questions.explanation: Reading the file triggers the mount. Checking the filesystem serving it distinguishes remote content from a local look-alike.

questions.stem: A new oneshot unit has been started but never enabled. It is active now. What has been established?
choices: It is guaranteed to start after reboot.
It ran this boot; its automatic activation still needs separate verification.
Its process must keep running indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Active and enabled describe different things. A oneshot can remain active after its program exits.

questions.stem: Why use a marker in /run to verify a service after reboot?
choices: Files there are permanently archived across boots.
All changes to /run are automatically written to the unit definition.
A new boot recreates /run, so something in this boot had to recreate the marker.
questions.explanation: A marker created in volatile runtime storage provides stronger evidence of a fresh service invocation than a file left on a persistent filesystem.

questions.stem: chronyd is active. Which observation best supports a claim that it is synchronizing with a particular source?
choices: chronyc sources -v shows that source as selected.
The chronyd unit file exists.
The designated source appears in /etc/chrony.conf.
questions.explanation: A selected source and tracking data show synchronization. A unit file or a configuration line cannot establish that the source was reachable.

questions.stem: The local hosts file supplies the name. Which check resembles a normal IPv4 application lookup?
choices: dig followed by a public resolver address
getent ahostsv4 followed by the hostname
ss -lnt on the server
questions.explanation: getent uses the guest name service configuration, including local files when configured. DNS-only queries can give a different answer.

questions.stem: An address added with ip is lost at reboot. Where should you record both IPv4 and IPv6 configuration on a NetworkManager guest?
choices: As a second ip address add command on the live interface.
In an ifup command typed at the current shell.
In the intended NetworkManager connection profile, with autoconnect verified.
questions.explanation: Profiles define persistent network configuration. Shell history and logs cannot reactivate addresses.

questions.stem: Which item should be installed on the target account for public-key SSH authentication?
choices: The client’s public key in that account’s authorized_keys.
The server’s public host key in the client account’s authorized_keys.
The client’s public key only in the client account’s known_hosts.
questions.explanation: The server checks proof that the client holds the matching private key. Only the public half belongs in authorized_keys.

questions.stem: After a firewalld reload a test opening vanished. What paired checks would have exposed this beforehand?
choices: Compare the runtime port listing twice in the default zone.
Query that port in the interface zone in both runtime and permanent configuration.
Query only the permanent rules for a different network zone.
questions.explanation: Reload replaces runtime state with permanent policy. Both stores and the zone must match the intended outcome.

questions.stem: Which pair makes a new custom web root recover its intended labels after restorecon?
choices: Change only the current file context with chcon.
Set the web service port type without updating the file mapping.
Define a persistent fcontext mapping, then apply it with restorecon.
questions.explanation: The mapping supplies the policy expectation for future relabels. restorecon applies that expected context to the existing tree.

questions.stem: A process requests mode 0666 with umask 027 and no default ACL. What is the resulting regular-file mode?
questions.explanation: The mask removes group write and all permissions for others. Regular-file creation did not request any execute bits.

questions.stem: A server task passed before reboot and failed afterward. What should your first retake investigation compare?
choices: Only the output captured before the first reboot.
Its startup configuration and new-boot journal against its observed live state.
Whether another guest currently has the right live configuration.
questions.explanation: The earlier check established a working live state. Startup configuration and logs can explain why the guest did not recreate it.

questions.stem: A VM starts the installer again after you finished installing. What would you inspect first?
choices: The learner's password expiry
The guest's firewall zone
Its virtual DVD attachment and boot order
questions.explanation: Booting from the ISO opens the installer before the installed system has a chance to start.

questions.stem: Which result confirms that your shell belongs to the intended Linux release?
choices: The laptop hostname contains the word redhat
The guest console reports ID=almalinux and a VERSION_ID of 10.x in /etc/os-release
Two virtual CPUs appear in the hypervisor
questions.explanation: Read the distribution ID and major version inside each guest. The host and the Linux provider have their own release files.

questions.stem: Bash shows a second prompt after you typed an opening quote. What happened?
choices: A second account has logged in
The shell is waiting for the closing quote
The command has been scheduled for later
questions.explanation: Quoting continues across lines until it is closed or canceled.

questions.stem: You need the exit status of a failed copy. When should you read it?
choices: Immediately after the copy
After listing the directory twice
Only after logging out
questions.explanation: The shell replaces the status after each command.

questions.stem: From ~/shift-practice/inbox which relative path reaches the archived copy?
choices: ../archive/day-one
./archive/day-one
/archive/day-one
questions.explanation: Two dots climbs one level before the walk continues into archive.

questions.stem: A service writes a marker under /run. What will a later boot do to this storage?
choices: Copy it to every user's home
Make every marker permanent
Recreate its runtime filesystem
questions.explanation: A marker there must be produced again on each boot if the service needs it.

questions.stem: Which manual section explains the fields in /etc/passwd?
choices: Section 1
Section 8 only
Section 5
questions.explanation: Section 5 covers file formats. Section 1 describes user commands.

questions.stem: Your editor reports that it saved. How can you check that only the intended line changed?
choices: Check that the editor process exited
Compare the edited copy with the saved original
Count the files in /etc
questions.explanation: A unified diff identifies the changed content and nearby context.

questions.stem: A pipeline produces a clean report but the terminal still shows “No such file”. Which stream carried the message?
choices: Standard input
Standard error
The report's standard output
questions.explanation: A normal pipe forwards stdout. A diagnostic can remain on stderr.

questions.stem: The file must retain yesterday's entries. Which redirect fits an append-only daily entry?
choices: 2> alone
questions.explanation: Appending preserves existing bytes; a single output redirect truncates an existing file.

questions.stem: An administrator confirms a file is group-readable. The reader belongs to that group but lacks search access on its parent. Which permission is missing?
choices: Search permission on the relevant directory
The file's modification time
The extension of the file name
questions.explanation: The kernel must resolve each directory on the path before checking the final file.

questions.stem: A file already existed when you changed umask. What happens to that file?
choices: It gains the new mask as a default ACL
It becomes executable
Its mode stays as it was
questions.explanation: Creation masks affect newly created objects.

questions.stem: sudo id -u prints 0. The same terminal then reports a nonzero number for id -u. Why?
choices: The terminal has logged out
The account was renamed twice
Privilege applied to the requested child command
questions.explanation: The parent shell retains its identity when the privileged command exits.

questions.stem: getent sees a new supplementary group but a running shell does not. Which test best follows?
choices: Recreate the account on the other guest
Start a fresh login as that user and run id
Change all files to mode 777
questions.explanation: The account database and an already running process can legitimately differ.

questions.stem: A client's name lookup returns loopback for a remote file server. Where would its TCP connection go?
choices: Directly to the server
Back to the client
To the default DNS server
questions.explanation: Loopback always refers to the machine making the connection.

questions.stem: Which observation shows whether a service accepts connections on a network address?
choices: The server's listening socket and bound address
The client's DNS search suffix
The text in the service description
questions.explanation: A socket bound only to loopback cannot receive a connection addressed to the server's LAN interface.

questions.stem: DNF lists a program in an available repository. Which check answers whether its RPM is installed here?
choices: Query the local RPM database by package name
Check the repository display name
Inspect the gateway address
questions.explanation: Availability in repository metadata and a local installation are independent facts.

questions.stem: A training shelf refreshes metadata but contains no packages. Which exercise can still succeed there?
choices: Install an application available only on the CDN
Upgrade every package to the latest CDN build
Validate the repository definition
questions.explanation: The empty shelf is sufficient for DNF to verify repository metadata.

questions.stem: Why can a second terminal's ps see a process that its jobs command cannot?
choices: ps lists only root-owned work
The process moved to another machine
Job tables belong to the launching shell
questions.explanation: The process table is system-wide, while each shell tracks its own jobs.

questions.stem: A service process returns with a new PID soon after it is terminated. What explains this?
choices: Its PID was written to DNS
Its service manager may have restarted it
A stopped process always restarts itself
questions.explanation: Supervisors can launch a fresh process according to the unit's policy.

questions.stem: A transient service was launched successfully but its program returned 1. Which evidence resolves the apparent contradiction?
choices: The number of CPU cores
The unit's recorded process exit status and journal
The shell prompt's hostname alone
questions.explanation: systemd can accept a launch request whose child program later fails.

questions.stem: Which filter selects yesterday's tagged message when the VM has rebooted exactly once since it was written?
choices: Previous boot plus the logger tag
Current boot plus a kernel filter
All boots sorted by PID only
questions.explanation: The boot selector identifies the run of the system and the tag identifies the message writer.

questions.stem: Which mechanism can make up a missed calendar run when a previously powered-off guest starts?
choices: A systemd calendar timer configured with Persistent=true
A bare interactive sleep command
Every regular cron entry automatically
questions.explanation: A persistent timer records the last trigger and can activate the service after downtime.

questions.stem: A per-user cron line includes learner just before the executable. What error is likely?
choices: The job automatically runs in two time zones
The time field becomes a username
Cron tries to execute a command named learner
questions.explanation: The username field belongs in a system crontab, not a per-user entry.

questions.stem: A script accepts quantities below ten as small. Which pair tests the exact boundary?
choices: 1 and 2
11 and 12
9 and 10
questions.explanation: The pair straddles the first value in the upper category.

questions.stem: Why emit the error to stderr and exit 2?
choices: All shell scripts must return 2 on success
A caller can keep data separate and detect invalid input
stderr changes the value of the argument
questions.explanation: Output streams carry text; exit status communicates success or failure separately.

questions.stem: vgs shows free extents while df reports a full XFS mount. How can both observations be true?
choices: df measures only unpartitioned disk
The free extents have not yet been assigned to that LV and filesystem
XFS can use all VG space automatically
questions.explanation: The volume group, logical volume and filesystem track capacity at different layers.

questions.stem: What identifies a new scratch disk most reliably in this lab?
choices: A before/after device inventory with matching size and no live data or mounts
Its name sorting last alphabetically
The first disk lsblk displays
questions.explanation: Device names can change. Correlating several observations reduces the risk of modifying the wrong device.

questions.stem: Firmware, the kernel and systemd all start, but a required data mount fails. Which evidence points most directly to the cause?
choices: Compare the device identity in fstab with the actual filesystem signatures
Reinstall the firmware first
Change the account's login shell
questions.explanation: A wrong mount identity prevents that unit from finding its device even on an otherwise bootable host.

questions.stem: Why verify both the running target and the configured default after this drill?
choices: Saving fstab always changes the default target
Rescue removes every installed kernel
A temporary boot choice can differ from the next normal startup
questions.explanation: Runtime boot arguments and the persisted target are distinct configuration layers.

questions.stem: Why can an ext4 mount still report its old capacity after lvextend succeeds?
choices: The new capacity always requires a new UUID
Mountpoints cannot grow without reformatting
The filesystem also needs to grow
questions.explanation: LV size describes the block device. ext4 maintains its own allocation structures.

questions.stem: Which observation demonstrates that an extension preserved application data?
choices: The second virtual disk is visible
The same file has the same checksum on the enlarged mounted filesystem
The VG contains two PVs
questions.explanation: An inventory proves topology; a content check on the correct mount tests the user's data.

questions.stem: What does an empty listing just after mounting a new volume prove?
choices: All underlying files were deleted
The newly mounted filesystem has no listed entries there
Every backup was moved to the new disk
questions.explanation: The mount changes which filesystem answers lookups at that directory.

questions.stem: A shell currently has the mountpoint as its working directory. What problem can this cause?
choices: The filesystem may be busy when you try to unmount it
Its UUID changes
Its filesystem type becomes tmpfs
questions.explanation: An active process reference can keep a mount busy.

questions.stem: A manual mount reads the export but accessing the autofs path fails. Where would you start?
choices: The client's autofs maps, trigger path and journal
Formatting the server disk
Resetting the client's local password
questions.explanation: Manual success establishes a working NFS path, leaving the automatic trigger as the difference.

questions.stem: Why change the marker on the server during diagnosis?
choices: It makes SELinux permissive
It changes the export address
A fresh change helps distinguish a live share from a stale local copy
questions.explanation: A local copy can match yesterday's text without accessing the server.

questions.stem: A client receives HTTP 403 for the specific page. Which fact does that establish?
choices: The client could not reach a TCP listener
The service's SELinux label is definitely correct
An HTTP server received the request and issued a response
questions.explanation: An HTTP status is evidence of application-layer communication. Authorization still needs investigation.

questions.stem: Local curl works, but after a firewall reload the private client times out. What should you compare?
choices: The webpage's text editor preference
Runtime and permanent HTTP rules in the actual interface zone
The previous user's shell history
questions.explanation: A runtime-only exception can disappear when firewalld reloads permanent settings.

questions.stem: After reboot the archive path exists but the marker has gone. Which check most directly explains the symptom?
choices: Compare the clients' time zones
Identify the mounted source and filesystem type serving that exact path
Count the user's supplementary groups
questions.explanation: A bare directory on the root filesystem can exist even when the intended data filesystem never mounted.

questions.stem: What evidence best proves the recurring receipt is configured and can run?
choices: A waiting timer after reboot plus a fresh event from the paired service
A unit file with the requested name
A screenshot of the text editor
questions.explanation: The schedule, its persistence and the actual work are three separately observable states.

questions.stem: Which command lists the lines of app.log that begin with ERR or WARN?
choices: grep '^ERR|WARN' app.log
grep -E '^(ERR|WARN)' app.log
grep -E '(ERR|WARN)' app.log
questions.explanation: Extended syntax treats | as alternation, and the parentheses keep the ^ anchor on both words. In basic syntax | is literal, and without ^ the last command also matches the words in the middle of a line.

questions.stem: A nightly command must append both its normal output and its errors to run.log. Which redirection does that?
choices: command >> run.log 2>&1
command 2>&1 >> run.log
command > run.log 2>&1
questions.explanation: Redirections apply left to right. Appending stdout first and then pointing stderr at it captures both. The second form leaves errors on the terminal, and the third overwrites the log.

questions.stem: You need a shell as fieldops with that account's own login environment and home directory. Which command gives it?
choices: su fieldops
su - fieldops
sudo fieldops
questions.explanation: The dash starts a login shell, which sets the target user's environment and working directory. Plain su keeps much of the caller's environment, and sudo expects a command to run.

questions.stem: You reset the root password from an rd.break shell on an SELinux-enforcing system. Which step before resuming startup prevents logins from failing afterward?
choices: Run setenforce 0 inside the chroot.
Create /.autorelabel so the next boot restores default file contexts.
Copy /etc/shadow to /etc/shadow- after changing it.
questions.explanation: The early shell runs without the loaded policy, so the new /etc/shadow can carry the wrong label. /.autorelabel makes the next normal boot restore default contexts. setenforce does not change file labels.

questions.stem: You ran mkswap on a new logical volume. Which /etc/fstab line activates it at every boot?
choices: UUID=<its UUID> none swap defaults 0 0
UUID=<its UUID> /swap xfs defaults 0 0
/dev/vdb swap swap noauto 0 0
questions.explanation: Swap has no mountpoint, so the second field is none and the type is swap. Activate it now with swapon -a, then confirm it in swapon --show. noauto would stop it activating at boot.

questions.stem: Which command sets a server's hostname so it survives a reboot?
choices: hostname files01
hostnamectl set-hostname files01
Adding files01 to /etc/hosts
questions.explanation: hostnamectl writes the static hostname. The hostname command changes only the running system, and /etc/hosts maps names to addresses without naming the machine.

questions.stem: A NetworkManager-managed interface needs a persistent DNS server. Where should you configure it?
choices: Edit /etc/resolv.conf directly.
Set ipv4.dns on the interface's connection profile and reactivate it.
Run resolvectl dns once on the interface.
questions.explanation: NetworkManager regenerates resolv.conf from the active profiles, so a hand edit can be overwritten. The profile property persists and applies when the connection comes up again.

questions.stem: One user wants new files to default to 640 in every future interactive shell. What makes that persistent?
choices: Run umask 027 once in the current shell.
Add umask 027 to that user's ~/.bashrc.
chmod 640 the user's home directory.
questions.explanation: umask applies to the shell that sets it and its children. A line in ~/.bashrc runs in each new interactive shell. Directory modes do not change the creation mask.

questions.stem: A file named late shift exists. Which command passes its complete name as one argument?
choices: printf '<%s>\n' late shift
printf '<%s>\n' "late shift"
printf '<%s>\n' late  shift
questions.explanation: Double quotes keep the embedded space inside one argument. Adding another unquoted space still separates the words.

questions.stem: You expected two .txt names and saw a literal *.txt. Both files exist in the current directory. What would explain the result?
choices: Both files were empty.
The program was found through PATH.
The pattern was enclosed in single quotes.
questions.explanation: Quoting keeps the shell from expanding the wildcard. File contents and the program's search path do not determine filename matches.

questions.stem: Where would you look up the fields in /etc/passwd?
choices: man 1 passwd
man 5 passwd
help passwd
questions.explanation: Section 5 documents file formats. The section 1 page explains a command a user can run.

questions.stem: A shell builtin changes the working directory. Where can you read its Bash-specific synopsis?
choices: rpm -q cd
cd /usr/share/doc/cd
help cd
questions.explanation: Bash supplies help for its builtins. A builtin does not require an executable or a separate RPM called cd.

questions.stem: A renamed file still changes when another name is used to edit it. Both are ordinary files on the same filesystem with the same inode number. Why?
choices: Both are independent copies with equal sizes.
Both names permanently store each other's path.
Both names address the same file through hard links.
questions.explanation: Hard links share the underlying object. Equal sizes alone cannot establish that relationship.

questions.stem: A symlink contains the text ../reports/current. Where does resolution of that relative target begin?
choices: In the directory containing the symlink
Always in the user's home
In the working directory of the user who created it
questions.explanation: A relative symlink is interpreted relative to its own parent directory when followed.

questions.stem: Why does a space after node2 matter in an anchored expression?
choices: It requests a case-insensitive comparison.
It marks the end of the hostname field and excludes node20.
It selects only files in the home directory.
questions.explanation: Anchoring alone distinguishes a prefix, not the end of a field. Matching its delimiter enforces the boundary.

questions.stem: grep produced no output and returned status 1 with a readable input file. What does that indicate?
choices: The input file is definitely missing.
A pattern match occurred on the previous boot.
The pattern selected zero lines.
questions.explanation: grep distinguishes no match from an error opening input. Check both status and diagnostic output.

questions.stem: A tar listing shows the filenames you expected. Which observation verifies the handoff more fully?
choices: The archive filename ends in .gz.
The archive is smaller than the source directory.
A fresh extraction compares equal to the source tree.
questions.explanation: Listing checks names; comparing a fresh restore checks file content as well.

questions.stem: Why use -C packet . when creating the archive?
choices: The archived names are relative to the directory being handed off.
It permanently changes the calling shell's working directory.
It forces all files to have identical owner and group.
questions.explanation: tar changes its own working directory for the named operands. The parent shell and source ownership stay as they were.

questions.stem: A restored link still begins with the old working directory's absolute path. Which independent check exposes the defect even if the old directory still exists?
choices: Inspect readlink on the restored link and require the relative target east-open.
Count the files in the original directory.
Compare the tar archive size with yesterday's archive.
questions.explanation: Reading through an absolute link may accidentally succeed while the source directory still exists. Inspecting the stored target tests portability.

questions.stem: Why repeat the ticket with west CLOSED?
choices: To convert the original gzip archive to bzip2.
To check whether the operator can adapt the selection rule to a new request.
To make the first restored file executable.
questions.explanation: The second data condition tests the decision behind the expression. Its expected output is different.

questions.stem: After sudo id reports uid=0, an ordinary whoami reports learner. What happened?
choices: The original account was renamed twice.
Only the child process ran with the authorized identity.
The terminal disconnected and logged in as a new guest.
questions.explanation: A one-command sudo invocation leaves the credentials of its calling shell intact.

questions.stem: Why can sudo echo text fail to redirect to a root-owned destination?
choices: echo can only print numbers under sudo.
Linux ignores ownership whenever the user has a terminal.
The original shell opens the redirection before sudo starts the command.
questions.explanation: Redirection is shell syntax. The identity of the process opening the file is what matters.

questions.stem: A user can rename a read-only file they own. Which permissions enabled that action in this exercise?
choices: Write and search on its parent directory
Execute on the file itself
Read access to the filesystem label
questions.explanation: Renaming changes directory entries. It does not rewrite the file contents.

questions.stem: A newly created ordinary file has mode 640 under umask 027. Why is its owner execute bit absent?
choices: The directory lacks an inode.
The creating program did not initially request execute for that file.
Only root can create executable files.
questions.explanation: A mask removes permissions from the requested mode. It cannot add an execute bit.

questions.stem: The lab has no default route. What makes a directly connected peer reachable anyway?
choices: A more specific route for the attached subnet
The DNS search suffix
The user's login shell
questions.explanation: The kernel chooses a matching route. A default route is needed only when no more specific route suffices.

questions.stem: Where should you look for the configuration NetworkManager will reuse on the next activation?
choices: The last ping result
The saved connection profile associated with the device
The shell prompt on the server
questions.explanation: Interface state shows what is active now. The profile supplies the settings used during activation.

questions.stem: Which observation establishes that tree is installed in this guest?
choices: A matching filename appears on the DVD.
A DNF repository refresh returns zero.
rpm -q tree reports an installed package version.
questions.explanation: The installed RPM database describes the guest. Package files and repository metadata can exist independently of installation.

questions.stem: DNF refuses the local RPM because its signing key is unknown. What should you establish before retrying?
choices: The expected signing identity and the authenticity of the source supplying its key
Whether the filename ends in .rpm
Whether the same file is readable by root
questions.explanation: DNF cannot authenticate a signature against an unknown trusted identity. Filename and file permissions do not resolve that trust question.

questions.stem: The learner installed an application with --user. Which observation identifies its configured source?
choices: rpm -q lists the guest kernel.
flatpak info --user for that app reports the origin under the same learner.
Another user has a desktop shortcut with the same name.
questions.explanation: Scope, identity and the app reference all matter. The installed app records its origin.

questions.stem: A runtime remains after removing the last course app. How should you clean up this exercise?
choices: Remove every runtime installed on the machine.
Delete the learner account to clear the program.
Verify it is the exercise's runtime, uninstall that reference and then remove the exercise remote.
questions.explanation: Flatpak stores shared runtimes separately. Confining cleanup to the references you introduced protects unrelated applications.

questions.stem: A process has been alive for two hours and shows very little CPU time. Which measurement includes time spent sleeping?
choices: CPU time charged to its instructions
Elapsed wall-clock time
Its nice value
questions.explanation: Elapsed time includes time spent waiting. It does not indicate that the process executed for two hours.

questions.stem: After renice changes NI from 0 to 10 for a normal process, what should you expect?
choices: Its memory allocation is cut in half.
It is guaranteed exactly ten percent of one CPU.
It competes less favorably for CPU when other runnable work exists.
questions.explanation: Niceness affects scheduling preference under contention. It is neither a memory limit nor a fixed CPU quota.

questions.stem: A oneshot prints its timestamp and exits zero, but status now says inactive. Which evidence supports a successful run?
choices: The timer simply has a filename ending in .timer
The service is continually using CPU
The timestamp entry and the service's last exit status
questions.explanation: A oneshot is expected to finish. The journal and exit status describe that execution.

questions.stem: You edited the calendar in /etc/systemd/system. How can you verify the manager is using the new schedule?
choices: Reload the manager, restart the timer and inspect its next firing.
Restart the system clock process and check the file date.
Only reread the unit text with cat.
questions.explanation: Reading the file confirms the edit. Reloading and checking the active timer confirms the scheduler has adopted it.

questions.stem: A display changes from 18:00 to 11:00 after changing TZ for one date command. What can you conclude?
choices: The NTP service corrected seven hours of drift.
The chosen presentation of the instant changed.
The server permanently changed its hardware clock.
questions.explanation: The TZ environment affects conversion for that process. It does not discipline the clock.

questions.stem: chronyd is active and every source remains marked ?. What evidence is missing?
choices: A graphical clock
A hostname containing the word time
A selectable reachable time source and successful synchronization
questions.explanation: An active process can poll unsuccessfully. Source and tracking data show whether it has usable measurements.

questions.stem: The timer is enabled and has a next run. The last service invocation exited 1. Is the delivery ticket complete?
choices: No. The schedule exists but the work failed, so inspect the service and its dependencies.
Yes. A future timer entry proves a file has been delivered.
Yes. Every enabled timer restarts the guest after a failure.
questions.explanation: Scheduling and successful execution are independently observable. The ticket requests an outcome from both.

questions.stem: Why can a one-time mkdir under /run appear to fix only the current boot?
choices: All directory names ending in audit are automatically removed every minute.
The runtime hierarchy is recreated at boot.
Enabling a timer always deletes its previous output.
questions.explanation: Persistent service configuration must arrange the runtime directory whenever the job needs it.

questions.stem: A script receives two quoted filenames, each containing spaces. Why should its inventory loop preserve the boundary of each positional argument?
choices: It converts each input to an absolute path.
It discards missing files automatically.
It keeps each supplied pathname as a separate argument, including spaces.
questions.explanation: The double-quoted dollar-at expansion passes each original argument as one word. A filename containing spaces reaches the loop as one item.

questions.stem: A missing file is followed by a valid file. Why keep result separate from the last command's exit status?
choices: The final result must remember an earlier failure even if later work succeeds.
Shell scripts cannot return zero.
wc always changes the original file.
questions.explanation: Each new command has its own status. The saved flag implements the program's whole-run contract.

questions.stem: You just created a GPT partition named reports. What else is needed before it can be mounted as an ext4 filesystem?
choices: Create ext4 inside the intended empty partition.
Add a DNS record called reports.
Change the partition's display name to /mnt/reports.
questions.explanation: GPT reserves a block range. The filesystem is a distinct structure that must exist before it can be mounted.

questions.stem: Which evidence shows the second partition was added without moving the first?
choices: The machine still has the same hostname.
The first entry has the same start and end in both partition-table listings.
The overall disk capacity is unchanged.
questions.explanation: The disk size does not show whether existing ranges moved. Comparing the first partition's boundaries checks that specific change.

questions.stem: A marker vanishes as soon as another filesystem is mounted over its parent directory. What changed?
choices: Mounting erased the original directory entries from disk.
Name lookup now enters the mounted filesystem at that location.
The original file was automatically copied to the new volume.
questions.explanation: A mount changes the filesystem reached through the path. Unmounting can reveal files underneath it.

questions.stem: Which result directly identifies the filesystem backing a particular report?
choices: The report's filename extension
The size of the directory listing
findmnt -T with the actual report pathname
questions.explanation: findmnt resolves the containing mount for the path; a name or size cannot identify its backing filesystem.

questions.stem: Which observation shows the kernel that the currently running guest actually booted?
choices: uname -r
The greatest version number printed by rpm -q kernel-core
The name of the default systemd target
questions.explanation: uname reads the running kernel's release. Installed and selected versions describe other parts of the boot process.

questions.stem: A unit fails after the root filesystem is mounted and other services start. Which evidence is most directly relevant?
choices: The size of the ISO download
The unit status and this boot's journal
The vendor name printed in the firmware menu
questions.explanation: The system manager has reached userspace and attempted the unit, so its status and journal narrow the failure.

questions.stem: The firewall query reports yes, but ss shows no listener on the port. What should you examine next?
choices: The intended service's startup, bind address and port
The file extension of the client's log
The user's time zone
questions.explanation: A firewall rule allows matching traffic through its policy. A service still has to accept a connection.

questions.stem: A client request succeeds before you add any rule. What conclusion is justified?
choices: The new rule definitely fixed a previously blocked request.
Something already permits the request, so the baseline cannot demonstrate that your new rule enabled it.
The service will automatically restart after a reboot.
questions.explanation: A comparison needs the initial behavior. An existing permissive zone or rule may already allow the traffic.

questions.stem: A readable document sits inside a parent that the service account cannot search. Which check exposes the first path failure?
choices: Compare web page titles.
Inspect ownership and search permission on each path component.
Count logical volumes on the server.
questions.explanation: The kernel checks traversal of each directory before it opens the final file. File read permission alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: Which test shows a confined web service can actually serve the corrected page?
choices: Read the file only from a root shell.
Change its name without checking the resulting type.
Request the exact URL from the client and verify the expected content under enforcing policy.
questions.explanation: The client exercises the listener, policy and service identity together. A root-shell read cannot demonstrate that path.

questions.stem: You remove a container, recreate it from the same image, and reattach the same named volume. Where should the retained line be found?
choices: In the reattached volume
In the removed container's private writable layer
In the host kernel command line
questions.explanation: The named volume has an independent lifetime. Reusing the image alone does not recover the first container's writes.

questions.stem: Why use --pull=never for this disconnected workshop?
choices: It prevents writes to the attached named volume.
It requires Podman to use an already available local image.
It converts the host into an image-mode installation.
questions.explanation: The pull policy controls image retrieval. It does not select the host's deployment model or make volumes read-only.

questions.stem: Root can read the marker. The unit declares User=erushift and Group=erushift. Which check best isolates the reported access failure?
choices: Run cat on the path under the erushift identity.
Reload systemd and repeat the root read.
List the user’s login shell as root.
questions.explanation: Testing as the consumer exercises its actual UID and groups along the full path.

questions.stem: The marker is root:erushift mode 0640 and its parent is root:erushift mode 0740. Why can the service group still receive a denial?
choices: Read permission on the file requires write permission too.
The group lacks search permission on the parent directory.
A service identity must have an interactive login shell.
questions.explanation: A process needs search permission on every directory component even when it knows the exact filename.

questions.stem: The repaired oneshot reports inactive after it runs. Which evidence establishes a successful run?
choices: The unit is enabled and its file exists.
The service account has a primary group.
Its exit status is zero and this boot’s journal contains the expected marker.
questions.explanation: A oneshot can exit and become inactive. Correlate its execution result with the observable work it performed.

questions.stem: Which sequence most directly demonstrates that the boot job works unattended?
choices: Reboot the server, confirm a different boot ID and find the correct unit message from this boot before starting it manually.
Restart the unit twice and show the same marker in each run.
Run daemon-reload after reboot and display the unit file.
questions.explanation: A manual restart can mask a missing enablement. The current-boot journal distinguishes a fresh run from old output.

references.title: Build your own client and server
references.body:
The supplied **rhcsa** profile in **Set up and reset the AlmaLinux 10.3 lab** creates the two machines and fixtures described here. If you used that profile, use the observations below to check your lab.

Use this guide when doing hands-on work on your own VMs alongside the browser lessons. The desktop app prepares its own isolated pair for machine grading. Your manually built pair can demonstrate the same outcomes. Save your evidence locally.

## Give the client and server a private link

Install two AlmaLinux 10 VMs from the installation lesson. Create learner as an administrator in both. Use separate installations so each has its own machine identity. Give each guest a NAT adapter for software access and add a second adapter connected to the same isolated virtual network. Leave the NAT profiles alone. Check that the lab's 192.168.77.0/24 subnet does not overlap a network you already use. If it does, choose a different private subnet for your manual pair and substitute your chosen addresses throughout. Keep a console open for network changes.

From the server console use `sudo hostnamectl set-hostname server`, then `nmcli device status`.

Identify the newly added private interface by its MAC address in your VM settings. Substitute its real name for IFACE below. Use these commands for an interface with no existing connection profile. If NetworkManager already created a profile for this interface, modify that specific connection with the same IPv4, IPv6 and autoconnect settings, then bring it up. Keep one active profile for the private interface.

On the client, set its hostname to client and repeat with 192.168.77.20/24. No gateway belongs on this private link. From each side use `ip route get PEER_ADDRESS` with the other address, then `ping -c 2 PEER_ADDRESS`. A ping response confirms an IP exchange; individual services need their own tests. The later dual-stack exercise uses a separate dummy interface. In both consoles verify `grep -E '^(ID|VERSION_ID)=' /etc/os-release` reports AlmaLinux major version 10.

## Give a fresh installation a real package source

On the AlmaLinux pair run `rpm -q almalinux-release` and `dnf repolist --enabled`.

Identify the baseos and appstream repository IDs. With network connectivity, refresh those sources with `sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=baseos --enablerepo=appstream makecache`.

AlmaLinux uses its own repositories and signing keys. The DVD alternative below supports offline work.

**RHEL exam transfer exercise.** Red Hat CDN access requires an entitled RHEL machine. On a RHEL installation attached to your Red Hat account, run `sudo subscription-manager identity` and `sudo dnf repolist --enabled`.

`subscription-manager` manages Red Hat subscription identity and repository access on registered RHEL guests.

Look for BaseOS and AppStream for your actual architecture. If your manual guest needs registration, use the installer’s Red Hat account connection or `sudo subscription-manager register` interactively with your authorized account.

List the available repository IDs with `sudo subscription-manager repos --list`.

Enable the matching BaseOS and AppStream IDs with `sudo subscription-manager repos --enable=ACTUAL_ID`. A CDN setup needs connectivity and an organization allowed to consume that content.

For an offline x86-64 manual guest you can instead attach the matching full AlmaLinux 10 DVD ISO as a virtual optical disk. A small boot ISO lacks the complete package trees. Use `lsblk -f` to identify the optical device.

Create the mountpoint with `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/alma-dvd`.

If the optical drive is /dev/sr0, use the terminal session.

Substitute the actual device and check that BaseOS/repodata/repomd.xml and AppStream/repodata/repomd.xml both exist. In a fresh /etc/yum.repos.d/lab-dvd.repo define two repository sections as below. Confirm the installed key path with `rpm -ql almalinux-gpg-keys` or `ls /etc/pki/rpm-gpg/`.

Use the AlmaLinux 10 signing key from your installed distribution. Keep the DVD mounted during package exercises, including after a reboot.

Use the terminal session, then query for a real package such as httpd on that source.

Use the same repository options on lab package transactions if unavailable network repositories are also configured. The metadata-only shelf below is a separate configuration exercise.

## Prepare the services used by the work orders

With AlmaLinux BaseOS and AppStream repositories available, use DNF to install the tools when you reach a workshop. On the client, the manual examples use autofs, nfs-utils, createrepo_c and openssh-clients. On the server they use nfs-utils, httpd, tuned, firewalld, chrony, policycoreutils-python-utils, openssh-server and curl. Install lvm2, xfsprogs, e2fsprogs, dosfstools, parted, at and cronie on the guest where you perform those workshops. Flatpak requires the flatpak package and an accessible remote. Keep SELinux enforcing. For identity exercises use fresh practice account and group names. Record any baseline settings before changing them.

On the manual server, start firewalld with `sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld`.

Check `sudo firewall-cmd --get-zones` and `sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --get-zones` for an unused zone name, shown as rhcsa-lab here.

Run `sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --new-zone=rhcsa-lab` and `sudo firewall-cmd --reload`.

From the console assign only the private profile with `sudo nmcli con mod lab-private connection.zone rhcsa-lab` and `sudo nmcli con up lab-private`.

Substitute the actual profile name if necessary. Check `sudo firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=IFACE` for both interfaces. Only the private adapter should report rhcsa-lab. Inspect other zones for prior permissions. To allow private SSH, use the terminal session and repeat with `--permanent`.

On the server, create /srv/projects with mode 0755 and make a world-readable file /srv/projects/erudior-lab.txt containing a short marker you choose. In a new file /etc/exports.d/shift.exports put this one line, substituting your private client address if needed.

Enable NFS with `sudo systemctl enable --now nfs-server`, apply the export with `sudo exportfs -ra` and inspect `sudo exportfs -v`.

For the NFSv4 client exercises, allow the nfs service in the server firewall zone used by the private interface. Verify the private zone with `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`.

Run `sudo firewall-cmd --zone=rhcsa-lab --add-service=nfs` and `sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=rhcsa-lab --add-service=nfs`.

Keep the firewall active. Test a read-only client mount and verify the source and marker using the NFS lesson. If using another subnet, adjust both the export rule and client mount address.

On the client prepare a metadata-only practice shelf with `sudo mkdir -p /srv/erudior-repo` and `sudo createrepo_c /srv/erudior-repo`.

`createrepo_c` builds RPM repository metadata for a directory.

Check for repodata/repomd.xml. This fixture is intentionally empty. For a real transaction use a trusted AlmaLinux repository or an approved signed package with its dependencies.

For the startup-service work order on the server, create /etc/systemd/system/erudior-maint.service with the service definition in the transcript, then reload systemd.

Leave it stopped and disabled for the learner to repair.

Confirm that TuneD lists the requested profile and that both guests boot normally. Take powered-off snapshots of this prepared state. For an independent run, start from those snapshots. Use normal lab accounts and fresh evidence. A course quiz or self-scored manual run records a different achievement from a desktop grader's before-and-after reboot checks.

## Supply time on the private pair

For the time-client workshop, use the untimed server as a local reference on the isolated practice network. Keep the values and copies from before the change. On the server, inspect `chronyc sources -n` and `sudo chronyd -p`.

`chronyd` runs the time synchronization daemon. Its -p option prints and parses the configuration.

If the pair has no upstream source, add `local stratum 10` to `/etc/chrony.conf` so the server can serve its own unsynchronized clock for this exercise. Permit the practice subnet with `allow 192.168.77.0/24`. Use the actual subnet if you built a different manual pair. Avoid duplicating an existing directive. Save and validate the configuration with `sudo chronyd -p` and restart chronyd.

Find the active zone of the interface carrying .10 using `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`.

Query the `ntp` service there before making a change. Where needed, add it to that zone at runtime and in permanent configuration. Confirm using both queries and check `ss -lun` for UDP port 123.

On the client add `server 192.168.77.10 iburst`, restart chronyd and wait for polling. An initial `^?` may change to `^*` as the client gathers samples. Compare `chronyc sources -n` on the client and `chronyc clients` on the server.

A local reference is for testing this isolated setup. In production choose an approved accurate time source. Restore both guests' original configurations and remove only the firewall rules you introduced.

## Terminal session

Follow the applicable console and package source in the notes. The first profile belongs on the server and the second on the client. The peer at .10 is tested from the client and the peer at .20 from the server. Subscription Manager is for an entitled RHEL guest. The optical drive and lab-dvd repository are for DVD installations. Configure exports, firewall and the startup unit on the server and the repository shelf on the client. Run the final sources check on the client and the clients check on the server. Read the instructions above before choosing steps.

```plaintext
>sudo hostnamectl set-hostname server

>nmcli device status
DEVICE  TYPE      STATE      CONNECTION
enp1s0  ethernet  connected  lab-private
>read -r -p "Unused private interface: " iface
Unused private interface: enp1s0
>sudo nmcli con add type ethernet ifname "$iface" con-name lab-private ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.77.10/24 ipv4.never-default yes ipv6.method disabled connection.autoconnect yes
Connection 'lab-private' (b7960b73-22bc-4dec-a2c0-e8676a158d23) successfully added.
>sudo nmcli con up lab-private
Connection successfully activated (D-Bus active path: /org/freedesktop/NetworkManager/ActiveConnection/3)
>sudo hostnamectl set-hostname client

>read -r -p "Unused private interface: " iface
Unused private interface: enp1s0
>sudo nmcli con add type ethernet ifname "$iface" con-name lab-private ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.77.20/24 ipv4.never-default yes ipv6.method disabled connection.autoconnect yes
Connection 'lab-private' (b7960b73-22bc-4dec-a2c0-e8676a158d23) successfully added.
>sudo nmcli con up lab-private
Connection successfully activated (D-Bus active path: /org/freedesktop/NetworkManager/ActiveConnection/3)
>ip route get 192.168.77.10
192.168.77.10 dev enp1s0 src 192.168.77.20 uid 1000
    cache
>ping -c 2 192.168.77.10
PING 192.168.77.10 (192.168.77.10) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.77.10: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.410 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.77.10: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.326 ms

--- 192.168.77.10 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1001ms
>ip route get 192.168.77.20
192.168.77.20 dev enp1s0 src 192.168.77.10 uid 1000
    cache
>ping -c 2 192.168.77.20
PING 192.168.77.20 (192.168.77.20) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 192.168.77.20: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.410 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.77.20: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.326 ms

--- 192.168.77.20 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1001ms
>grep -E '^(ID|VERSION_ID)=' /etc/os-release
ID="almalinux"
VERSION_ID="10.3"
>rpm -q almalinux-release
almalinux-release-10.3-15.el10.x86_64
>dnf repolist --enabled
repo id       repo name
baseos        AlmaLinux 10 - BaseOS
appstream     AlmaLinux 10 - AppStream
>sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=baseos --enablerepo=appstream makecache
Metadata cache created.
>sudo subscription-manager identity
```
